findings.headline: Reserves, assets and liabilities that will transfer with Fire and Rescue are still being confirmed and are not included in SBSA's reserves.
findings.detail: The transferring reserves, pension liabilities and other long-term commitments are being confirmed with East Sussex Fire Authority and West Sussex County Council. The position will be set out in the final budget report, and the same work will be done for other functions before they transfer.
findings.matters: Transferring pension liabilities and reserves are a balance sheet question that a lender or finance director would need to see before judging SBSA's financial position after the transfer.
findings.quote: pension liabilities and other long-term commitments, are being confirmed with East Sussex Fire Authority and West Sussex County Council

findings.headline: The Mayoral Capacity Fund grant of £2.8m in 2027/28 is an estimate based on the published formula, and will be confirmed in the local government finance settlement.
findings.detail: The grant is a key income line for SBSA's budget. Other recent government announcements, including the Autumn Budget capacity funding and Good Growth Fund money, are not yet built into the draft.
findings.matters: A finance director at another mayoral authority will want to know which grant lines are still estimates and which are confirmed, because the budget depends on these figures before the February settlement.
findings.quote: The Mayoral Capacity Fund grant of £2.8 million in 2027/28 is an estimate based on the published formula for newer mayoral authorities.

findings.headline: Transition costs are £0.83m in 2026/27 and £1.21m in 2027/28, against the £2 million estimated in the Quarter 1 report.
findings.detail: The paper describes these figures as broadly in line with the Quarter 1 estimate. Of the 2027/28 costs, £879k is funded, including £380k from the transition reserve set aside in 2026/27, and the remaining transition funding requirement is still to be reconciled.
findings.matters: A one-off transfer cost that has been estimated at £2m and is now being planned at a lower annual figure, with part of it funded from reserves, shows how a new authority is paying for its own set-up.
findings.figures: £0.83m in 2026/27; £1.21m in 2027/28; £2 million estimated at Quarter 1; £879k funded in 2027/28; £380k from transition reserve
findings.quote: Table 6 shows transition costs of £0.83m in 2026/27 and £1.21m in 2027/28, broadly in line with the £2 million estimated in the Quarter 1 report.

findings.headline: SBSA's draft revenue budget is balanced in every year of the Medium-Term Financial Plan to 2030/31, on current assumptions.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan shows total expenditure matched by income in every year, with net expenditure of zero. The paper notes that the position will be refined as funding allocations and the costs of transferring functions are confirmed.
findings.matters: A new strategic authority showing a balanced multi-year plan, while transferring functions and grant allocations are still unsettled, is a position other finance officers and lenders would want to compare with their own.
findings.figures: £52.9m SBSA draft expenditure in 2027/28; £93.2m in 2028/29; £91.3m in 2029/30; £91.4m in 2030/31; net expenditure nil in each year
findings.quote: The MTFP presents a balanced position to 2030/31 on current assumptions

findings.headline: East Sussex Fire and Rescue's draft budget shows a £1.1m gap in 2027/28, rising to £2.4m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: East Sussex Fire and Rescue has net expenditure of £56.5m in 2027/28 against funding of £55.3m. The service is preparing options to balance 2027/28, and further work is needed on later years.
findings.matters: An unbalanced fire budget transferring to a new fire authority, with no agreed closing measures, is a funding question that other councils and lenders would track before the February precept decision.
findings.quote: East Sussex has a £1.1m gap in 2027/28, and work is continuing to identify measures to balance the position before the final budget and precepts are set.

findings.headline: The estimated cost of the May 2028 mayoral election has increased from around £4m to £6m, with the election reserve raised to £2m by March 2028.
findings.detail: The previous budget assumed contributions of £500,000 a year to the election reserve against an expected cost of about £4 million. The proposed contributions rise to £1m in both 2026/27 and 2027/28, and the draft 2028/29 budget assumes £2m from the reserve and £4m of revenue provision.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, can compare how an authority is funding a one-off election cost that has risen by half through reserves, revenue and later rebuilding contributions.
findings.figures: around £4m; £6m; £500,000 a year; £1m; £2m by March 2028; £1.5m a year from 2028/29; £4.5m by March 2031
findings.quote: The estimated cost of the 2028 mayoral election has increased from around £4m to £6m.

findings.headline: West Sussex Fire & Rescue Service's draft budget shows a funding gap of nil in each year from 2027/28 to 2030/31, with total funding equal to net revenue expenditure.
findings.detail: The draft balances in every year. In 2027/28 it relies on a £1,700k reduction in back-office costs and a £1,000k amount covered by additional precept. A corporate provision / contingency of £500k is included in each year.
findings.matters: A finance director at a peer council can see a fire service with a balanced four-year draft and identify the specific balancing items, including the back-office reduction and the use of additional precept.
findings.figures: Funding gap / (surplus): nil in 2027/28 to 2030/31. Net revenue expenditure £51,699k (2027/28), £57,496k (2030/31). Reduction in back-office costs £1,700k (2027/28). Covered by additional precept £1,000k (2027/28). Corporate provision / contingency £500k in each year.
findings.quote: Table A2: West Sussex Fire & Rescue Service (£'000)

findings.headline: East Sussex Fire & Rescue Service's draft budget shows a funding gap of £1,122k in 2027/28, rising to £2,360k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The table shows net revenue expenditure exceeding total funding in every year. The 'Covered by additional precept' row is blank (–) for all four years. Recurring pressures are £4,593k in 2027/28, against new opportunities and savings of £1,204k.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare a fire service's gap trajectory with its own, and a lender can see that the draft plan does not yet show a measure closing the gap in any year.
findings.figures: Funding gap / (surplus): £1,122k (2027/28), £1,410k (2028/29), £1,880k (2029/30), £2,360k (2030/31). Recurring pressures £4,593k (2027/28). New opportunities and savings £(1,204)k (2027/28). Council tax precept £(38,473)k (2027/28) rising to £(43,556)k (2030/31).
findings.quote: Table A1: East Sussex Fire & Rescue Service (£'000)

findings.headline: The budget consultation runs from 10 December to 22 January, with the Board's final budget decision on 17 February.
findings.detail: Findings and changes will be reported to the Committee on 3 February before the Board decides. For future years, a January decision depends on whether the settlement, consultation and scrutiny can all be completed in time.
findings.matters: The timetable, and the risk that a January decision slips to February, is a deadline finance officers elsewhere will recognise.
findings.quote: Public consultation is proposed from 10 December to 22 January.

findings.headline: An £800k Adult Skills Fund top-slice is included for 2027/28, with transport grants passed to councils in full.
findings.detail: Where SBSA administers a grant and the conditions allow, it keeps a share to cover its costs. Grant income is included only where receipt is considered likely.
findings.matters: The top-slice is a retained amount from a grant, and the rule for what is kept versus passed on is a point other councils administering grants will compare.
findings.figures: £800k Adult Skills Fund top-slice (2027/28)
findings.quote: For 2027/28 this includes an £800k Adult Skills Fund top-slice.

findings.headline: The draft pay assumption is 3.3% for 2027/28 and 3.0% a year after, with each percentage point on pay costing SBSA about £70k a year.
findings.detail: Non-pay costs use contract rates where known and 2% elsewhere. A 2-point change in pay would be about £140k, up or down.
findings.matters: A pay award assumption and a per-point sensitivity figure are the inputs a finance director would test against their own pay settlements.
findings.figures: 3.3% pay award 2027/28; 3.0% a year thereafter; about £70k per percentage point; about £140k for 2 points
findings.quote: The draft assumes a 3.3% pay award in 2027/28, reflecting recent local government pay settlements, and 3.0% a year after that.

findings.headline: Grant funding is held at 2028/29 levels, with no additional government funding beyond the current settlement assumed in later years.
findings.detail: The paper says much of SBSA's funding is specific grant passed to partners or ring-fenced, so grant changes would largely change what is passed on rather than SBSA's own costs. The MTFP will be updated if funding changes.
findings.matters: Holding funding flat from 2028/29 is an explicit planning assumption that peer councils and lenders would compare against their own settlement assumptions.
findings.quote: The draft MTFP assumes no additional government funding beyond the current settlement and holds funding at 2028/29 levels in later years.

findings.headline: The draft assumes no new borrowing in SBSA's own revenue budget, and interest of £349k is assumed on forecast cash balances in 2027/28, with no interest income in later years.
findings.detail: The paper states that the fire services carry their own capital financing costs within their budgets. Borrowing, PWLB and MRP matters will be covered in the capital and treasury proposals.
findings.matters: The absence of borrowing in the revenue budget, and the removal of interest income after 2027/28, both shape the treasury position that lenders and finance officers review.
findings.figures: 4% interest on forecast cash balances; £349k estimated income in 2027/28
findings.quote: SBSA's own revenue budget does not assume new borrowing.

findings.headline: The Investment Fund is set at £7.6m of revenue and £7.6m of capital in 2027/28, rising to £19m of each from 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2027/28 allocation is largely committed to existing programmes and programme pipeline development. New proposals will be presented to the Board under the Local Assurance Framework.
findings.matters: A step up from £7.6m to £19m in both revenue and capital is a large planned increase in discretionary spending that peers and lenders would track.
findings.figures: £7.6m revenue; £7.6m capital (2027/28); £19m revenue; £19m capital (from 2028/29)
findings.quote: The MTFP assumes £7.6m of revenue and £7.6m of capital Investment Fund in 2027/28, rising to £19m of revenue and capital respectively a year from 2028/29.

findings.headline: The draft assumes no funding from Rewiring the State, with allocations and the allocation methodology yet to be confirmed by government.
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFP will be updated once allocations are confirmed. Government plans are described as still in development.
findings.matters: Any future allocation is an income line that is currently excluded from the budget, which is relevant to lenders and finance officers assessing the funding base.
findings.quote: The draft MTFP therefore assumes no funding from Rewiring the State.

findings.headline: The May 2028 mayoral election is now costed at about £6m, to be met from the election reserve and planned 2028/29 revenue.
findings.detail: The paper says the draft provides for the cost through the election reserve and planned 2028/29 revenue, subject to confirmation. Annual contributions will then rebuild the reserve for the following election.
findings.matters: A one-off cost of about £6m drawn against a reserve, with the reserve then rebuilt, is a reserve movement that finance officers at other councils will want to compare.
findings.figures: about £6m
findings.quote: Updated information puts the cost of the May 2028 mayoral election at about £6m.

findings.headline: The draft budget includes a general reserve benchmark of about 5% of controllable spending, reflecting SBSA's stage of development.
findings.detail: The paper links the benchmark to SBSA building the organisation and taking on new functions. The Section 73 Officer's statutory assessment of estimates and reserves will accompany the final budget.
findings.matters: A finance director compares reserve benchmarks across councils, and the statutory S73 assessment will be the formal test of whether the reserves are adequate.
findings.figures: about 5% of controllable spending
findings.quote: The draft proposes a general reserve benchmark of about 5% of controllable spending

findings.headline: The draft MTFP provides a £500k SBSA revenue contingency and £1.207m of identified transition costs in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The contingency is for unforeseen costs from the transfer of Fire and Rescue and other functions. The paper states that fire service contingencies are not available to support wider SBSA transition costs, and that the adequacy of these provisions will be kept under review.
findings.matters: Transition costs and the size of the contingency against them are central to how a new combined authority budget is being built and will be watched by peers facing similar transfers.
findings.figures: £500k revenue contingency; £1.207m transition costs in 2027/28
findings.quote: The draft MTFP assumes a £500k SBSA revenue contingency to meet unforeseen costs arising from the transfer of Fire and Rescue and other functions.

findings.headline: East Sussex draft fire budget shows a £1.122m funding gap, with West Sussex's draft balanced on current assumptions, so the combined draft shows a £1.122m gap.
findings.detail: The paper gives net expenditure of £56.464m for the East Sussex fire budget and £51.699m for West Sussex. Work with both services is continuing ahead of the final budget.
findings.matters: An unfunded gap in a fire budget that is being transferred to SBSA is a live pressure for the finance director and for any peer council or lender assessing the new authority's position.
findings.figures: £1.122m funding gap; £56.464m net expenditure (East Sussex); £51.699m net expenditure (West Sussex)
findings.quote: The East Sussex draft has net expenditure of £56.464m and a £1.122m funding gap.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX 2 - Financial Expenditure and Forecast Outturn final_
findings.headline: East Sussex records that the Queensway Gateway Road Levelling-Up Partnership grant was £2.5m, one of several funding sources totalling £4.175m.
findings.detail: The paper lists MHCLG Levelling-Up Partnership funding of £2.5m, East Sussex Highways capital of £0.811m and Section 106 contributions of £0.047m and £0.817m as match funding. It states that the historic £10m Local Growth Fund is not a new receipt available for ESCC's completion costs.
findings.matters: A council sourcing gap-funding for a scheme taken over from a failed developer would want to see which grant and developer contributions were actually counted against the completion cost.
findings.figures: MHCLG LUP grant £2,500,000; ESCC Highways capital £811,000; S.106 £47,000 and £817,000; total match funding £4.175m
findings.quote: including a £2.5m Levelling-Up Partnership contribution from the then Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX 2 - Financial Expenditure and Forecast Outturn final_
findings.headline: East Sussex's 2026/27 close-out provision for Queensway Gateway Road is £0.5m, of which £0.17m had been recorded by 27 October 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the provision covers contractor close-out commitments and ESCC professional commissions, and remains sensitive to corrective works and outstanding compensation-event or dispute assessments. It states that a verified final outturn cannot yet be confirmed.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know how much of a close-out provision has been drawn so far, and how far the final account remains open.
findings.figures: 2026/27 close-out provision £500,303 (£0.5m); recorded at 27.10.2026 £0.17m
findings.quote: The current finance tracker for the close-out and subsidiary works is currently £0.17m (27.10.2026), against a budget of £0.5m.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX 2 - Financial Expenditure and Forecast Outturn final_
findings.headline: East Sussex's indicative cumulative Queensway Gateway Road expenditure is £7.882m, against £4.175m of identified match funding, leaving £3.707m to be met from other capital financing.
findings.detail: The paper says the £3.707m balance is a funding balance rather than a further construction cost, and that the required funds have been identified and committed across several capital and revenue programmes. It describes the £7.882m as indicative until Finance completes its reconciliation.
findings.matters: A finance officer elsewhere would see a capital scheme funded partly from unspecified council capital and revenue programmes, with the shortfall described as identified but not yet reconciled.
findings.figures: Indicative cumulative expenditure £7.882m; match funding £4.175m; balance £3.707m
findings.quote: Compared with the indicative cumulative expenditure of £7.882m by October 2026, this leaves approximately £3.707m to be met through other County Council capital financing arrangements

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX 2 - Financial Expenditure and Forecast Outturn final_
findings.headline: East Sussex's 2025/26 Queensway Gateway Road spend came in at £4.494m against a £5.316m budget, a £0.822m variance.
findings.detail: The paper reports that commercial scrutiny, subcontractor account review and resolution of compensation events reduced 2025/26 expenditure below budget. It also states the variance is not necessarily a saving against the contractual target or final project cost.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council facing a target-cost contract with a compensation-event tail would want to see how a year-end underspend was achieved and how far it is treated as a real saving.
findings.quote: Actual expenditure was £4.494m, an underspend of £0.822m against that financial year budget.

findings.headline: Net pension liability down £3.1m to £31.7m at 31 March 2026, with the Fund moving to the Border to Coast pool from 1 April 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the decrease was driven by remeasurements and that a £47.1m asset ceiling adjustment under IFRIC 14 reduced the pension asset. It also says the Fund moved from ACCESS to Border to Coast after the government stopped supporting ACCESS.
findings.matters: A council moving its pension fund to a new investment pool is a transition other councils with pension funds will be running in parallel.
findings.figures: Net pension liability £31.7m (from £34.7m); decrease £3.1m; asset ceiling reduction £47.1m
findings.quote: has decreased by £3.1m from £34.7m at the start of the year to £31.7m at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Cash balances reduced by 46% during 2025/26; investment income of £4.5m at an average return of 4.51%
findings.detail: The average funds available for investment were £99.8m. The paper says investment returns stayed above the Bank of England base rate, which fell from 4.50% to 3.75% over the year.
findings.matters: A 46% fall in cash balances reduces the investment income base that other councils and lenders see as a source of cash flexibility.
findings.figures: Cash balances reduction 46%; average funds available £99.8m; investment income £4.5m; average return 4.51%; base rate 4.50% to 3.75%
findings.quote: cash balances have reduced significantly in recent years due to ongoing financial challenges, with a reduction of 46% during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Funding expected to reduce by under £13m over the three-year settlement period to 2028/29
findings.detail: The paper attributes the reduction to the Fair Funding Review 2.0 outcome, which shifted resources toward areas with higher deprivation. It says 2026/27 funding is broadly flat in cash terms and a real-terms reduction given inflation.
findings.matters: A multi-year funding reduction from a national formula change is one finance directors at other councils will be modelling on the same basis.
findings.figures: Funding reduction 'just under £13m' over three years to 2028/29
findings.quote: East Sussex is expected to experience a reduction in funding of just under £13m over the three-year settlement period to 2028/29.

findings.headline: Dedicated climate change budget ended in February 2025 after the council decided it 'could no longer afford' one; £7.933m spent on climate projects to 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says new climate capital spending stopped in July 2024 and that remaining spend completes earlier projects. It shows total spend of £7.933m against £7.933m of funding, leaving no remaining funding.
findings.matters: A council stating it can no longer afford a dedicated climate budget is a specific cut other councils with similar pressures will compare.
findings.figures: Total climate spend £7.933m (2021/22 to 2026/27 estimate); allocated budget £6.005m; grants £1.928m; original additional funding £9.9m
findings.quote: it could no longer afford to have a dedicated climate change budget

findings.headline: 2026/27 capital programme of £101.5m, with £30.0m funded by borrowing
findings.detail: The paper sets out the 2026/27 capital resources as borrowing, scheme-specific grants, non-specific grants, reserves and receipts. It describes the programme as based on an assumption of significantly reduced future funding.
findings.matters: The size of the borrowing element in the capital plan is what lenders will assess against the council's stated borrowing position.
findings.figures: Planned 2026/27 capital investment £101.5m; borrowing £30.0m; scheme-specific grants £26.1m; non-specific grants £38.1m; capital reserves and revenue contributions £2.9m; capital receipts £4.4m
findings.quote: As per the approved budget at February 2026, the County Council plans to invest £101.5m in capital projects in 2026/27, funded by:

findings.headline: Capital spend of £93.0m gross against a revised budget of £97.9m, with £63.7m net
findings.detail: The paper says slippage occurred across projects and that inflation and material costs led to some projects being paused and reassessed to stay within approved budgets.
findings.matters: Projects paused for inflation reasons are a delivery pressure other councils face in their own capital programmes.
findings.figures: Gross capital spend £93.0m; revised budget £97.9m; scheme-specific resources £29.3m; net expenditure £63.7m
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the County Council spent £93.0m gross, of which £29.3m was funded by scheme-specific resources, giving net expenditure of £63.7m.

findings.headline: No additional long-term borrowing in 2025/26; external debt of £200.1m, all held with PWLB at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the council used internal reserves to finance its capital programme during a period of relatively high interest rates. It says further debt restructuring is being monitored.
findings.matters: A council choosing reserves over new borrowing during high rates is a funding choice other councils and lenders are watching.
findings.figures: External debt £200.1m, all PWLB at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: No additional long-term borrowing was undertaken during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Non-PWLB loan of £6.45m, maturing October 2058, repaid early at a 'favourable discount' in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says a Barclays Market Loan was repaid in 2025/26 with support from MUFG. The remaining non-PWLB loan was then repaid early from available balances, and the paper estimates savings of about £0.1m per year over 10 years. The paper does not state the Barclays loan's amount or whether it was a LOBO.
findings.matters: Early repayments of market loans from cash balances change the council's funding and interest profile, and lenders and other councils will compare the discount achieved.
findings.figures: Non-PWLB loan £6.45m, maturing October 2058; estimated savings approximately £0.1m per annum over the next 10 years
findings.quote: The remaining non-PWLB loan (£6.45m, maturing in October 2058) was also repaid early using available balances, at a favourable discount.

findings.headline: General fund balance of £10.0m at 31 March 2026, 2.7% of the net revenue budget against a 2.5% target minimum
findings.detail: The general fund balance was unchanged at £10.0m during the year. The paper treats it as a minimum balance, backed by a general contingency that was fully applied in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A general fund at 2.7% of budget against a 2.5% target is a specific measure finance directors compare across councils.
findings.figures: General fund balance £10.0m; actual 2.7% against target 2.5%; general contingency for 2026/27 £6.7m
findings.quote: is in line with the target minimum level of 2.5% (actual 2.7%) of the net revenue budget set by the Council.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves projected to reduce to £3.9m by 2030, described in the paper as 'unsustainable'
findings.detail: The paper says the projection underlines the need for action if government funding is not forthcoming. Strategic, service and other earmarked reserves were £56.1m at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: A reserve projected to fall to £3.9m is a direct measure of how much buffer remains for other councils and for lenders assessing resilience.
findings.figures: Strategic reserves projected £3.9m by 2030; earmarked reserves at 31 March 2026 £56.1m
findings.quote: Strategic reserves are projected to reduce to £3.9m by 2030, which is unsustainable and underlines the need for actions to be taken if government funding is not forthcoming.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support approved in principle, with the Council to borrow to balance the 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The paper says reserves are now at the minimum level required and the council has sought Exceptional Financial Support. It describes the borrowing as not sustainable and as adding future liabilities.
findings.matters: Borrowing to balance a revenue budget is a funding position a lender and other councils' finance officers will want to track against the approval terms.
findings.figures: Structural deficit for 2026/27 £55.6m
findings.quote: Approval in principle has been received, and the Council will therefore need to borrow to balance the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £55.6m for 2026/27 after £6.3m of savings
findings.detail: The 2026/27 annual budget deficit is £44.2m, and the £11.4m carried forward from 2025/26 brings the total to £55.6m. Budget growth of £71.7m is set against £21.2m of additional funding and £6.3m of savings.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this size with reserves at minimum levels is the funding gap a finance director elsewhere would need to close and a lender would need to see funded.
findings.figures: Structural deficit £55.6m; annual budget deficit £44.2m; carried forward £11.4m; budget growth £71.7m; savings £6.3m; additional funding £21.2m
findings.quote: a structural budget deficit of £55.6m exists for 2026/27.

findings.headline: High Needs Block recovery grant, a repayment of 90% of cumulative DSG deficits, to be received in autumn 2026 and not recognised in 2025/26
findings.detail: The grant is conditional on approval of the SEND Reform Plan and additional scrutiny of council accounts and financial returns. The paper says it is therefore not recognised in the 2025/26 accounts.
findings.matters: Whether the grant arrives depends on conditions the council does not yet control, which affects how much of the DSG deficit will be repaid.
findings.figures: Grant repayment 90% of cumulative DSG deficit as at end 2025/26; cumulative DSG deficit £19.8m
findings.quote: East Sussex will receive the grant in autumn 2026, therefore it is not recognised in the 2025/26 accounts.

findings.headline: Cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £19.8m at 31 March 2026, the first year the Council has been in a cumulative DSG deficit
findings.detail: The deficit has been moved to the Dedicated Schools Grant Adjustment Account in Unusable Reserves under the statutory override. The balance sheet section gives the reserve as £19.9m.
findings.matters: A cumulative DSG deficit is a balance sheet item that lenders and finance directors at other councils are tracking, and this is the first year the council has reported one.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £19.8m; balance sheet DSG reserve deficit £19.9m
findings.quote: This is the first year that the Council has been in a cumulative DSG deficit

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £9.98m and Children's Services by £10.12m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Adult Social Care overspend to rising demand and more people being supported, with lower average package costs. Children's Services cost pressures relate to placements for Children We Care For and Home to School Transport.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends in both social care services are the pressure most councils are reporting, and the paper gives the unit-cost position alongside the volume position.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care overspend £9.98m; Children's Services overspend £10.12m
findings.quote: Adult Social Care overspent in 2025/26 by £9.98m, primarily due to an increase in demand and more people being supported

findings.headline: £11.45m planned and £9.67m additional draws from reserves used to offset the service overspend
findings.detail: The paper describes both draws as one-off funding that cannot be used again. It says this affects future years' financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Reserves drawn to cover a current overspend cannot cover the same pressure next year, which affects how other councils judge their own reserve use.
findings.figures: Planned draw £11.45m; additional draw £9.67m; total £21.12m
findings.quote: A planned draw of £11.45m plus an additional draw of £9.67m from Reserves have also been used to offset the service overspend; this is one-off funding that cannot be used again

findings.headline: Service overspend of £20.25m offset by a £19.82m underspend in Corporate Budgets, with all general contingency applied
findings.detail: The paper says the corporate underspend arose because the whole general contingency was needed to offset pressures. Treasury Management also underspent by £3.69m.
findings.matters: Using the full general contingency leaves no in-year buffer, which is relevant to any council planning on the same contingency.
findings.figures: Service spend variation £20.25m; Corporate Budgets underspend £19.82m; Treasury Management underspend £3.69m; general contingency for 2026/27 £6.7m
findings.quote: The service overspend was offset by an underspend of £19.82m in Corporate Budgets, where all the General Contingency budget was required to be applied

findings.headline: 2025/26 net outturn of £580.05m against a revised net budget of £579.62m, a net overspend of £0.43m
findings.detail: The council reports a net outturn overspend of £0.43m after service budgets overspent by £20.25m. Corporate budgets were used to absorb most of the service overspend.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a £20m service overspend was held to under £0.5m at year end, and at what cost to reserves.
findings.figures: Net outturn £580.05m; revised net budget £579.62m; net overspend £0.43m; service spend variation £20.25m
findings.quote: net outturn at year end was £580.05m against a revised net budget of £579.62m, a net overspend of £0.43m.

findings.headline: Year-end capital commitment enquiries cover amounts over £10m, and the auditor recommends extending them below that threshold.
findings.detail: Project leads are asked whether they expect capital spend above £10m at year end and respond no if not. The auditor warns that individually immaterial commitments could be material in aggregate, and recommends enhancing the enquiry to capture significant commitments below the threshold.
findings.matters: Capital commitments below £10m can add up to a material sum, which matters to any council planning its capital programme and borrowing.
findings.figures: £10m disclosure threshold
findings.quote: the Council only include amounts over £10m in their financial statements.

findings.headline: Pension fund asset value given to the actuary was £15.5m different from the figure in the IAS 26 report, creating an unadjusted disclosure misstatement.
findings.detail: The estimated impact on the Council is approximately £5,321,614. The net pension asset is unaffected because an equal and opposite adjustment is made to the asset ceiling, so only the Note 42 disclosure is affected. The Council concluded the misstatement was immaterial and the auditor agrees.
findings.matters: The opening asset value fed to the actuary drives the pension disclosures, and other councils relying on the same inputs could face the same question.
findings.figures: £15.5m difference; £4,974,695k actuary asset value; £5,321,614 estimated Council impact
findings.quote: the actuary was provided with a more up-to-date asset value of £4,974,695k as of 31 March 2025 leaving a difference of £15.5m to the whole fund.

findings.headline: Impaired debt provision percentages could not be supported with workings, as ESCC was unable to provide documentation for how they were originally calculated.
findings.detail: The percentages were derived when the impairment methodology was first developed. The auditor recommends better document retention and at least an annual review of the impairment percentages. Management says the workings behind any revised calculation will be shared with the auditors.
findings.matters: A bad debt provision that cannot be evidenced is a provision that lenders and other finance directors cannot test against recovery experience.
findings.quote: However, ESCC was unable to provide the supporting workings and documentation evidencing how these percentages were originally calculated.

findings.headline: Auditor reports that no responses were received from councillors, many of whom have since left following the recent election, on registers of interest.
findings.detail: The auditor found the related parties register may not be up to date. It recommends stronger controls to ensure registers of interest and annual declarations are completed by all councillors.
findings.matters: Incomplete councillor registers are a governance control that other councils' auditors would test after an election.
findings.quote: many have since left the council because of the recent election and no responses were received.

findings.headline: High Needs Block recovery grant final payment expected in 2026/27 is £17.860m, following approval of the SEND Reform Plan.
findings.detail: The grant was previously shown as a contingent asset in the draft accounts. The final version of the accounts updates the disclosure to say the plan has been approved, and the same information is added to the events after the balance sheet date note.
findings.matters: The amount and timing of high-needs recovery funding is relevant to other councils with high-needs funding pressures.
findings.figures: £17.860m (final payment expected)
findings.quote: confirmed that the final payment expected is £17.860m.

findings.headline: Auditor expects an unqualified opinion, identifies no material uncertainty related to going concern, and plans to issue the audit report in the first week of December 2026.
findings.detail: The work is substantially complete, subject to internal reviews, a signed management representation letter, and review of the final financial statements. The certification of closure is being delayed until the NAO has concluded its Whole of Government Accounts work.
findings.matters: The opinion, going concern conclusion and sign-off timing are the first things a lender or finance director checks for the 2025/26 accounts.
findings.figures: first week of December 2026 (expected report date)
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be unqualified based upon the completed work to date and subject to satisfactory completion of the above outstanding points.

findings.headline: Two of three prior-year audit recommendations have been implemented; the gross internal area and land area records issue remains open.
findings.detail: The Schools PFI liability recalculation point has been implemented. The GIA and land area issue persists, with the Council saying it still has an ongoing project to remeasure GIAs. The auditor notes a similar control environment deficiency in the current year.
findings.matters: Repeated gaps in property evidence are the kind of finding that councils with large estates would compare against their own asset records.
findings.figures: 2 of 3 prior-year recommendations implemented
findings.quote: We are pleased to report that management have implemented 2 of our recommendations, however 1 issue still remains.

findings.headline: Manual journal authorisation threshold is £1 million, which the auditor describes as slightly higher than other councils.
findings.detail: Journals below the threshold can be posted without formal review or authorisation. The auditor raised a best practice recommendation to reassess the threshold and consider independent review below it. Management's response says it is confident the current threshold and review processes would detect any material errors, and will keep the threshold under review.
findings.matters: Journal authorisation thresholds are a management override control, and the auditor's comparison with other councils gives peer finance teams a benchmark.
findings.figures: £1 million threshold
findings.quote: we noted that the Council applies a £1 million threshold to require journals authorisation prior to posting.

findings.headline: Creditors sample testing found 3 items with issues, projecting an overstatement of the creditor balance of £2,063k.
findings.detail: One item was paid before year end but still reported as payable. The auditor recommends a formal review of the creditors process and stronger year-end controls, and has raised a control deficiency over the review of year-end expenditure and creditors balances.
findings.matters: A control deficiency in the year-end expenditure review is the kind of finding other councils' auditors may test for in the same way.
findings.figures: 3 items; £2,063k projected overstatement
findings.quote: The impact of these 3 items has led to a projected overstatement of the creditor balance of £2,063k

findings.headline: Unadjusted errors have a net impact of £749k on the CIES and £2,063k on the general fund reserve, which the auditor treats as immaterial.
findings.detail: The errors comprise a projected creditor overstatement of £2,063k and a Home Office UASC and care leavers grant of £1.314m recognised in 2025/26 that related to 2024/25 services. The auditor says the grant item is correctly accounted for within the general fund.
findings.matters: The general fund figure is the number a finance director would reconcile against reported reserves, and the auditor has left it uncorrected.
findings.figures: £749k (CIES net impact); £2,063k (general fund reserve impact); £1.314m (UASC grant)
findings.quote: We also identified errors which have a net impact on CIES of £749k and impact on general fund reserve of £2,063k.

findings.headline: Social Care Grant reclassified from non-specific grant income to specific grant under cost of services, with 2024/25 comparatives restated.
findings.detail: The grant terms require it to be used for adult and children's social care, so it should have been credited to services. The Council restated 2024/25 because the grant was material in that year. The paper says there is no impact on the deficit or reserves.
findings.matters: How a grant is presented between cost of services and non-specific income changes the reported service cost picture, which other councils with similar grants would compare.
findings.quote: The Social Care Grant was incorrectly classified as an un-ringfenced grant

findings.headline: The Oracle ledger, in use from 1 April 2025, produced one significant issue: 8 users in the Oracle support team assigned new access roles to their own accounts without formal approval.
findings.detail: The ledger moved from SAP to Oracle on 1 April 2025, while SAP continues to be used for payroll, pensions and procurement. The auditor says there is a risk that users could gain unapproved access to the ledger and change figures, and full details will be in a separate IT findings report.
findings.matters: A new ledger that allows self-assigned access without approval is a control weakness that other councils moving systems would want to check.
findings.figures: 8 users; 1 significant issue
findings.quote: Our audit work identified 1 significant issue with the Oracle system, which relates to the Absence of a Formal Process Governing Self-Assigned Access within Oracle Fusion.

findings.headline: Value for money work reports one significant weakness in arrangements, relating to use of exceptional financial support (EFS).
findings.detail: The weakness sits under financial sustainability in the value-for-money work, which is covered in a separate Auditor's Annual Report presented alongside this one. The auditor also raised an improvement recommendation to support the Council's DSG arrangements.
findings.matters: Use of exceptional financial support is a financial sustainability matter that other finance teams and lenders will look at directly.
findings.figures: 1 significant weakness in arrangements; 1 key recommendation; 1 improvement recommendation
findings.quote: One significant weakness in arrangements was identified and a key recommendation made relating to use of exceptional financial support (EFS).

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation decisions paused by central government in September 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the council had made notable progress preparing for the transition, including political and officer oversight and increased resourcing. It identifies funding as a key risk to delivering the programme.
findings.matters: A pause to reorganisation decisions changes the timetable and funding assumptions for councils going through LGR, and affects how finance directors plan for transition costs.
findings.quote: September 2026, when central government announced a pause to LGR decisions

findings.headline: Pension Fund assessed at 117% funded, with a £0.75bn surplus, at the 31 March 2025 valuation
findings.detail: The paper says the Fund's assets exceed the level required to cover liabilities, and that investment management charges were slightly below the average of a comparison group of schemes over three years.
findings.matters: A funding level above 100% is a clear indicator of pension fund solvency that lenders and finance directors at other administering authorities will compare.
findings.figures: 117% funded; £0.75bn surplus; 0.521% average investment management charges vs 0.586% comparator average
findings.quote: assessing the Fund to be 117% funded, with a £0.75bn surplus

findings.headline: Orbis Internal Audit formally separated from the shared partnership on 1 May 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the council is moving to a shared internal audit model with Brighton and Hove City Council and has exited the Orbis Inter-Authority Agreement for other services, reverting to a sovereign model.
findings.matters: Councils that share services through partnerships such as Orbis face the same disaggregation questions, and the transition is a practical precedent for them.
findings.quote: Orbis Internal Audit formally separated on 1 May 2026

findings.headline: Management confirmed there is currently no central or corporate oversight of contract performance
findings.detail: The paper says the council introduced a refreshed Contract Management Framework and Playbook in 2025/26, but that oversight remains devolved to services and the sovereign procurement function is still being embedded. It raises improvement recommendation 2.
findings.matters: Without corporate oversight of contracts, a council may not identify supplier or service performance problems early, which other councils with similar contract portfolios will want to test.
findings.quote: management confirmed that there is currently no central or corporate oversight of contract performance

findings.headline: Changes to the funding formula reduce funding by £12.6m over the period
findings.detail: The paper says the unfavourable outcome from the Fair Funding Review is one of the factors contributing to the council's projected budget deficits.
findings.matters: Fair Funding changes that remove funding from a specific council are the kind of revenue shift that other councils will want to compare against their own settlements.
findings.figures: £12.6m reduction in funding over the period
findings.quote: Changes to the funding formula have resulted in a reduction of £12.6m in funding over the period

findings.headline: Auditor retains a "significant weakness" finding on financial sustainability and updates key recommendation 1
findings.detail: The paper says the council's ability to balance budgets relies on exceptional financial support. Key recommendation 1 asks the council to reduce reliance on EFS over time.
findings.matters: A key recommendation on financial sustainability is the highest-level value-for-money finding, and it is the same reason councils nationally are being assessed on EFS dependence.
findings.quote: We consider that a significant weakness within financial sustainability remains

findings.headline: Auditor anticipates an unqualified opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements after the November 2026 Audit Committee
findings.detail: The paper says the audit is substantially complete and that no significant adjustments affecting the primary statements have been made to the draft accounts. It also says there were no written statutory recommendations or Public Interest Report.
findings.matters: An unqualified opinion on time, after draft accounts were submitted to the national deadline, is a signal of accounts quality that finance directors and lenders look for.
findings.quote: We anticipate issuing an unqualified audit opinion following the Audit Committee meeting in November 2026

findings.headline: Exceat Bridge construction has been broadly on track since approval of a revised plan
findings.detail: The paper says major cost and delivery pressures on the project were identified, reported and corrected through Cabinet scrutiny. It says the Place Scrutiny Committee is providing active oversight of the remaining work.
findings.matters: A single major scheme that has had cost pressures and a revised plan is a case other councils with similar projects can compare their own delivery against.
findings.quote: Following the approval of a revised plan, construction has been broadly on track

findings.headline: £93.0m (95.0%) of capital expenditure delivered in 2025/26 against approved budget of £97.9m
findings.detail: The paper says slippage was carried into future years of the capital programme. The auditor considers the level of slippage modest and not indicative of weaknesses in capital programme management.
findings.matters: Capital delivery against budget shows how far the programme is holding to its plan, which other councils and lenders compare when assessing borrowing-funded capital.
findings.figures: £93.0m capital expenditure; 95.0% of approved budget; £97.9m approved budget
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council delivered £93.0m (95.0%) of capital expenditure against approved budget of £97.9m.

findings.headline: Central government to fund 90% of the DSG deficit accrued to 31 March 2026, leaving a £2.0m residual deficit
findings.detail: The paper says the cumulative DSG deficit was £19.8m at the end of 2025/26, the first year the council reported a deficit, and that forecasts show it rising. It also says the council will still be expected to fund part of residual deficits over the statutory override period.
findings.matters: Government support covering most of the accrued DSG deficit, with the remainder still on the balance sheet, is the mechanism other councils with high-needs deficits will be assessing.
findings.figures: 90% of deficit funded; £19.8m cumulative DSG deficit at end 2025/26; £2.0m residual deficit; £93.0m forecast 2027/28
findings.quote: Central government have confirmed funding of 90% of the deficit accrued to 31 March 2026

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget includes £6.3m of savings, equal to 0.9% of the net revenue budget
findings.detail: The paper says this level of planned savings is low relative to the overall budget requirement and is insufficient to make a meaningful contribution to closing the projected gaps.
findings.matters: A savings figure set against the net revenue budget shows how much of the gap is being addressed through efficiencies, a comparison that matters to peers and lenders.
findings.figures: £6.3m savings in 2026/27 budget; 0.9% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget includes £6.3m of savings. The level of planned savings remains low relative to the overall budget requirement (0.9% of the net revenue budget)

findings.headline: £12.2m (85.3%) of the £14.3m 2025/26 savings target delivered, with £1.9m slipping to future years
findings.detail: The paper says £0.2m was not achieved but replaced with other permanent savings. It also says the proportion of savings achieved against target has increased year on year.
findings.matters: The gap between savings targets and delivery shows how far planned savings are landing, and the year-on-year trend is a comparison other finance officers can use.
findings.figures: £14.3m savings target; £12.2m (85.3%) delivered; £1.9m slipped; £0.2m replaced
findings.quote: The Council identified a savings target of £14.3m for 2025/26. At year-end, £12.2m (85.3%) was delivered, with £1.9m slipping to future years and £0.2m not achieved but replaced with other permanent savings.

findings.headline: Unplanned reserve draw of £9.7m at 2025/26 outturn, in addition to an £11.4m planned draw
findings.detail: The paper says the unplanned draw used several earmarked reserves, including the capital reserve, the collection fund surplus, insurance reserves and the LGR reserve. It says this reduces the capacity to manage future risks.
findings.matters: Drawing on earmarked reserves such as the capital and LGR reserves reduces the buffer available for future pressures and transformation, which other councils and lenders will look for.
findings.figures: £9.7m unplanned draw; £11.4m planned draw
findings.quote: resulting in an unplanned draw on reserves of £9.7m in addition to the £11.4m planned draw at budget setting for a balanced budget.

findings.headline: MTFP shows deficits of £80.7m in 2027/28 and £117.7m in 2028/29, with reserves of £59.2m at end of 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper cites the medium-term financial plan presented to Cabinet in June 2026. It sets the forecast deficits against projected total reserves, which fall to £48.8m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare forecast deficits with projected reserve balances to judge how long the council could cover gaps before needing further support.
findings.figures: £80.7m deficit 2027/28; £117.7m deficit 2028/29; £59.2m reserves end 2026/27; £48.8m reserves end 2029/30
findings.quote: The MTFP (as presented to Cabinet in June 2026) identified a £80.7m deficit in 2027/28 and a £117.7m deficit in 2028/29, with total reserve levels estimated to be £59.2m at the end of 2026/27 and falling further to £48.8m by the end of 2029/30.

findings.headline: Council anticipates further EFS in 2027/28, with a current ballpark figure of over £100.0m
findings.detail: The paper says the 2027/28 requirement is likely to exceed the £70.0m requested for 2026/27. It notes that the council is expected to need further EFS to balance that budget.
findings.matters: A second year of EFS at this scale would be a material call on government support, and lenders and peers will track whether the amount is confirmed.
findings.figures: over £100.0m ballpark for 2027/28 EFS; £70.0m requested for 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council already anticipates requiring further EFS in 2027/28 to be able to balance the budget - the amount required will likely be an escalation from the £70.0m requested in 2025/26, with a current ballpark figure of over £100.0m.

findings.headline: EFS borrowing costs forecast at £1.8m in 2026/27, rising to £4.7m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper explains that the capitalisation directive operates as emergency borrowing rather than grant funding, so the council bears financing costs on the EFS amount.
findings.matters: The cost of financing EFS is a recurring revenue charge that rises in the following year, which lenders and finance directors need to factor into the medium-term position.
findings.figures: £1.8m borrowing costs in 2026/27; £4.7m in 2027/28
findings.quote: These borrowing costs are therefore forecast to be £1.8m in 2026/27, increasing to £4.7m in 2027/28.

findings.headline: £70.0m of exceptional financial support approved for 2026/27, with budgeted use of £55.6m and a £14.4m contingency
findings.detail: The application was made to central government to balance the 2026/27 budget. The paper says the budget gap was identified early in the budget process and could not be closed by savings or reserves without undermining financial resilience.
findings.matters: EFS is a capitalisation direction, so a council relying on it is financing revenue spending through borrowing, and other councils and lenders will watch the scale of approvals.
findings.figures: £70.0m EFS; £55.6m budgeted use; £14.4m contingency
findings.quote: To balance the 2026/27 budget, an application for £70.0m of EFS was requested from central government, which includes budgeted use of £55.6m and a contingency of £14.4m.

findings.headline: Service overspend of £20.2m in 2025/26, 3.6% of approved net budget, down from £21.9m (4.2%) in 2024/25
findings.detail: The paper records the overspend as a slight improvement on the prior year. It attributes the overspend mainly to demand and cost pressures in children's services and adult social care.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can compare the size of the overspend, its share of net budget, and the service areas driving it against their own position.
findings.figures: £20.2m service overspend; 3.6% of approved net budget; £21.9m prior-year overspend; 4.2% of approved net budget
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council reported a service overspend of £20.2m (3.6% of approved net budget), representing a slight improvement on the £21.9m overspend (4.2% of approved net budget) recorded in the previous year.

findings.headline: Some data migration defects will be carried forward into Hypercare after go-live, according to the Chief Operating Officer.
findings.detail: The Chief Operating Officer updated the subgroup on the volume of data migration defects and said a number of them would be carried forward and dealt with during Hypercare. The 6 November minutes record that some risks remain ahead of go-live, with resources focused on priority issues such as where pay is affected.
findings.matters: Defects carried into the post-go-live support period are a specific control exposure in payroll migrations, and other councils can check how their own migration plans handle them.
findings.quote: a number of these will be carried forward and dealt with during Hypercare

findings.headline: The Corporate Management Team made a risk-based decision on 14 October 2026 to proceed to Cutover.
findings.detail: The Chief Operating Officer told the subgroup that the Corporate Management Team took the decision to proceed to Cutover on 14 October 2026, with the risks of go-live described as data migration quality and build quality remaining a concern. Later minutes record that the Corporate Management Team agreed to continue towards go-live on 22 October 2026.
findings.matters: It shows the decision-making route for proceeding with a major system cutover while risks are still open, which other councils facing similar choices can compare against.
findings.figures: decision date 14 October 2026
findings.quote: Team had made a risk-based decision to proceed to Cutover

findings.headline: Parallel payroll run PPR3 achieved a 97.64% match against a 99% threshold, and PPR2 was closed having missed its threshold by less than 1%.
findings.detail: The subgroup was told that PPR1 met its 80% threshold. A decision was then taken to close PPR2 despite the target threshold being missed by less than 1%. For PPR3, the Chief Operating Officer said the variances arose from data quality issues rather than Oracle payroll calculation defects.
findings.matters: Parallel-run match rates are the evidence a finance director relies on before accepting a new payroll system, and a council closing a run below threshold is a decision other councils would want to see the reasoning for.
findings.figures: PPR1 threshold 80%; PPR2 missed threshold by less than 1%; PPR3 match 97.64% against a threshold of 99%
findings.quote: a decision was taken to close PPR2 despite the target threshold being missed by less than 1%.

findings.headline: The paper estimates delaying go-live, and running SAP and Oracle together, would cost in excess of £5 million.
findings.detail: The Chief Operating Officer told the subgroup that delaying go-live and running SAP and Oracle simultaneously would have an estimated cost implication above £5 million. This estimate was given in the 9 October 2026 minutes, when the subgroup discussed risks associated with delaying go-live.
findings.matters: It gives a finance director a sized figure for the cost of a dual-running delay on a major system migration, which can be used when weighing go-live timing.
findings.figures: in excess of £5 million (estimated)
findings.quote: delaying go-live and running SAP and Oracle simultaneously would have an estimated cost implication in excess of £5 million

findings.headline: East Sussex completed Oracle cutover on 4 November 2026, and the November payroll is the first to run on Oracle.
findings.detail: The Chief Operating Officer confirmed that cutover finished on 4 November 2026 and that the November payroll will be the first payroll run on the Oracle system. The 9 October minutes had planned the move to cutover for 16 October 2026, and the 22 October minutes record SAP as decommissioned on 16 October 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council running a similar SAP-to-Oracle payroll migration can compare this cutover timetable and the number of parallel runs against their own plan.
findings.figures: Cutover completed 4 November 2026; planned cutover 16 October 2026; SAP decommissioned 16 October 2026
findings.quote: RP confirmed that Cutover was completed on 4 November 2026.

findings.headline: Forecast interest on long-term debt for 2026/27 is approximately £10.3m and is within the budgeted provision.
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast interest paid on long-term debt for the year is approximately £10.3m and sits within the budgeted provision. Total borrowing at 30 September 2026 was £194.642m at an average rate of 4.30%, all from the PWLB.
findings.matters: Debt interest that stays within budget while the council is reducing its external borrowing matters to finance directors and lenders assessing the cost of the council's existing debt.
findings.figures: approximately £10.3m forecast interest; £194.642m total borrowing; 4.30% average rate
findings.quote: is approximately £10.3m and is within the budgeted provision

findings.headline: The average investment balance was £44m in Q1 and Q2 2026/27, which the paper describes as the lowest average level for over a decade.
findings.detail: The paper says available balances averaged at the lowest level for over a decade. Short-term deposits are being reinvested for up to three months at fixed rates of 3.97% to 4.25%, and the report notes ongoing reductions in balances.
findings.matters: Declining average balances are a direct sign of the reserve drawdown that peer finance officers and lenders track alongside the council's deficit position.
findings.figures: £44m average investment balance to September 2026; £43.8m average for Q1 and Q2; 3.97% to 4.25% fixed deposit rates
findings.quote: Balances available in the period have averaged at the lowest level for over a decade.

findings.headline: The strategy forecasts internal borrowing of at least £75.000m in 2026/27, drawn from reserves and balances.
findings.detail: The paper says the medium-term level of reserves and balances allows for internal borrowing of at least £75.000m in 2026/27, meaning internal resources are used in place of external borrowing. This is the basis for the forecast new borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Reserves covering a large share of the borrowing need is a position a finance director would test against the council's risk, and lenders would test against its liquidity.
findings.figures: at least £75.000m internal borrowing; £140.058m expected new borrowing; £215.058m total new borrowing requirement
findings.quote: The Strategy currently forecasts that the level of reserves and balances in the medium term allows for internal borrowing

findings.headline: The treasury strategy was prepared alongside a deficit revenue budget forecast and an application for Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper states that the 2026/27 strategy was prepared in the context of the deficit revenue budget forecast and the EFS application, and that the capitalisation direction has been built into the treasury strategy. Capitalisation direction is forecast at £70.000m, and the paper describes a reduction in available balances.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support funded through capitalisation direction is a route other councils facing deficits may also use, and its effect on treasury planning is set out here.
findings.figures: £70.000m capitalisation direction borrowing requirement; deficit forecast in the MTFP to 2028/29
findings.quote: deficit revenue budget forecast and application for EFS in 2026/27

findings.headline: New borrowing of £140.058m is expected during 2026/27 to support the capital programme and capitalisation direction.
findings.detail: The Q2 forecast Capital Financing Requirement gives a new borrowing requirement of £215.058m, made up of £145.058m for the capital programme and £70.000m for capitalisation direction. Internal resources are expected to cover part of this, and the timing of any borrowing will depend on the wider position.
findings.matters: The size of the new borrowing requirement, and the share of it driven by capitalisation direction, is the figure a lender or peer council would need to assess the council's future funding need.
findings.figures: £140.058m new borrowing; £215.058m total new borrowing requirement; £145.058m capital programme; £70.000m capitalisation direction; total CFR £409.700m
findings.quote: It is therefore expected that new borrowing of £140.058m may be required to support the capital programme and capitalisation direction during 2026/27

findings.headline: The average investment return of 3.95% in Q1 and Q2 2026/27 beat the 3.73% benchmark by 0.22 percentage points.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the outperformance to the interest rate outlook and to investments placed at higher rates that have not yet matured. Forecast investment income for 2026/27 is £1.8m, depending on cash flow and rates.
findings.matters: A council reporting returns above its benchmark while balances are shrinking is a point of comparison for other councils managing similar cash positions.
findings.figures: 3.95%; 3.73%; 22 basis points (0.22 percentage points); investment income £0.9m to September 2026; forecast £1.8m for 2026/27
findings.quote: The average investment return during the period was 3.95% over-performing the benchmark rate by 22 basis points

findings.headline: Two PWLB loans of £2m and £3.5m, both at 7.125%, matured in the half year and were not replaced, in line with a strategy to use reserves to fund borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper says the two PWLB loans matured on 30 June and 30 September 2026 and that the maturing debt was not replaced. The next PWLB maturity is £1.5m at 6.50% on 30 June 2027.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, would want to know that external debt is falling because maturities are being met from reserves rather than new borrowing.
findings.figures: £2m; £3.5m; 7.125%; external borrowing £194.642m at 30 September 2026; next maturity £1.5m at 6.50%
findings.quote: This maturing debt was not replaced to maintain the strategy to maximise use of reserves to initially fund borrowing

findings.headline: Maximising internal borrowing is expected to reduce investment balances and investment income
findings.detail: The paper notes the trade-off that using cash to fund borrowing lowers investment balances and therefore investment income. The paper also says investment balances were expected to reduce as cash is used to support borrowing.
findings.matters: The trade-off between lower borrowing costs and lower investment income is a choice other councils also make when using reserves in place of external borrowing.
findings.figures: none given in the paper for this point
findings.quote: Maximising internal borrowing will reduce investment balances and therefore investment income.

findings.headline: Cash and investment balances were expected to fall to support the borrowing need
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction in cash and investment balances was expected because reserves are being used to support borrowing. The risk appetite for investments was kept unchanged while the security of funds was prioritised.
findings.matters: A planned fall in cash balances reduces the council's investment income and changes its liquidity position, which finance officers and lenders would both track.
findings.figures: none given in the paper for this point
findings.quote: Cash balances and therefore investment balances were expected to reduce to support the authority’s borrowing need.

findings.headline: The paper says the investment strategy 'appropriately contributes to mitigating' the Council’s deficit revenue position
findings.detail: The strategy was set against the deficit revenue budget forecast for 2025/26 and the medium-term financial plan for 2026/27 to 2028/29. The paper says the risk appetite for investments was not changed to increase income.
findings.matters: Treasury management is being cited as part of a deficit-mitigation plan, which other councils with deficits may compare against their own approaches.
findings.figures: none given in the paper for this point
findings.quote: The Investment Strategy appropriately contributes to mitigating the Council’s deficit revenue position.

findings.headline: The liability benchmark indicates external borrowing could be avoided until 2026/27, with borrowing for day-to-day activity possible by 2029/30
findings.detail: The benchmark assumes internal borrowing of cash-backed reserves and balances while keeping a buffer. The paper says the timing depends on reserve balances continuing to decrease as currently anticipated.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would see the point at which the council's reserve-funded position is expected to end and external borrowing to become necessary, including for day-to-day spending.
findings.figures: external borrowing avoidable until 2026/27 (year); possible day-to-day borrowing by 2029/30 (year)
findings.quote: the Council may need to borrow to finance day-to-day activity in addition to its capital programme by 2029/30.

findings.headline: Officers used the Council’s own reserves cash to initially fund borrowing, with around £75m of internal borrowing modelled in the longer term
findings.detail: The paper says internal borrowing reduced cash balances, counterparty risk and borrowing costs. The strategy is to maximise internal borrowing while interest rates are high, and the level is kept under review.
findings.matters: Using reserves in place of external borrowing is a choice other councils facing similar capital pressures would weigh, and it changes the council's future external funding need.
findings.figures: around £75m internal borrowing in the longer term
findings.quote: Officers utilised cash from the Council’s own reserves to initially fund borrowing.

findings.headline: East Sussex's 2025/26 to 2027/28 borrowing need is £29m, after a capital programme review reduced the requirement by £65m from £94m originally planned
findings.detail: The paper says the borrowing need followed a review and reprofiling of the Capital Programme, with the objective of minimising borrowing costs within the Treasury Management revenue budget. The review is the stated reason for the reduction.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would see a large reduction in the planned borrowing requirement and how it was achieved through capital reprofiling.
findings.figures: £29m borrowing need over 2025/26 to 2027/28; £65m reduction; £94m originally planned
findings.quote: This review reduced the borrowing requirement by £65m from £94m originally planned for the period between 2025/26 and 2027/28.

findings.headline: The council's total capital financing requirement, including PFI and finance leases, was £408m in 2025/26 and is estimated to fall to £398m by 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper states that the 2025/26 CFR included PFI schemes and finance leases totalling £95m, leaving an underlying need to borrow of £313m. The forecast shows a £4m reduction in 2026/27, a £2m increase in 2027/28 and an £8m reduction in 2028/29.
findings.matters: The forecast path of the CFR indicates whether the council's future borrowing requirement is expected to rise or fall, which drives its need for new funding.
findings.figures: Total CFR £408m (2025/26 actual), £404m (2026/27 estimate), £406m (2027/28 estimate), £398m (2028/29 estimate); PFI and finance leases £95m; underlying need to borrow £313m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 actual Capital Financing Requirement of £408m included PFI Schemes and Finance Leases totalling £95m, excluding these balances the underlying need to borrow was £313m.

findings.headline: East Sussex County Council received £4.498m of short-term investment interest in 2025/26 at an average rate of 4.51%, against an average SONIA of 4.04%.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the council's monthly investment rate was above the SONIA benchmark in every month of the year, with the annual margin at +0.47%. Monthly investment balances fell from £647k in April to £132k in March.
findings.matters: Investment income is a budget line that moves with cash balances and rates, and a falling balance alongside a rate margin shows how the council's internal borrowing and cash position interact.
findings.figures: £4.498m total interest; average rate 4.51%; average SONIA 4.04%; margin +0.47%; average monthly amount £647k in April falling to £132k in March
findings.quote: The total amount received in short -term interest for the year was £4.498m at an average rate of 4.51%.

findings.headline: East Sussex County Council's external borrowing stayed within its operational boundary and authorised limit in 2025/26, with £85.858m of headroom under the operational boundary.
findings.detail: The paper states that external borrowing at 31 March 2026 of £200.142m, which includes temporary short-term borrowing, was under both the operational boundary of £362.000m and the authorised limit of £382.000m. Headroom under the operational boundary, after PFI and leases, was £85.858m.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders use these limits to judge how much additional borrowing the council can take on without breaching its approved framework.
findings.figures: Operational boundary £362.000m; authorised limit £382.000m; PFI and leases £76.000m; underlying limit £286.000m (operational boundary) and £306.000m (authorised limit); external borrowing £200.142m; headroom £85.858m (operational boundary) and £105.858m (authorised limit)
findings.quote: The Operational Boundary and Authorised limit have not been exceeded during the year.

findings.headline: Closing capital financing requirement reached £312.966m in 2025/26 against a £276.672m estimate, while external borrowing stood at £200.142m at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reports an in-year borrowing requirement of £26.571m against an estimate of £15.812m, and an opening CFR of £292.380m against an estimate of £268.971m. The gap between the CFR and external borrowing, shown as the under-borrowing position, was £112.824m against an estimated £76.530m.
findings.matters: A larger gap between the CFR and external borrowing means more of the council's borrowing need is being met from cash balances rather than external loans, which affects when and how much new funding it will need to raise.
findings.figures: CFR £312.966m outturn; £276.672m original estimate; external borrowing £200.142m; under-borrowing £112.824m outturn vs £76.530m estimate; in-year borrowing requirement £26.571m vs £15.812m estimate; opening CFR £292.380m vs £268.971m estimate; MRP £5.985m vs £8.111m estimate
findings.quote: Closing CFR 276.672 312.966

findings.headline: Short-term interest received in 2025/26 was £4.5m at an average rate of 4.51%, against a SONIA benchmark of 4.04%.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the above-benchmark performance to the investment portfolio being locked into higher-rate investments during a falling base rate environment. The Bank of England cut Bank Rate three times in the year, to 3.75% from 18 December 2025.
findings.matters: Locking in fixed-term deposits ahead of rate cuts is a specific approach other councils can compare against their own investment returns.
findings.figures: £4.5m interest received; average rate 4.51%; SONIA benchmark 4.04%; Bank Rate 3.75% from 18 December 2025
findings.quote: The total amount received in short term interest for 2025/26 was £4.5m at an average rate of 4.51%.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing was taken in Q4 2025/26 to cover temporary cash flow shortfalls, and the NatWest overdraft outstanding at 31 March 2026 was repaid in early April 2026.
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing was sourced from the local authority market through approved brokers or as an authorised overdraft with the council's bank, NatWest. The overdraft was repaid in full in early April 2026. The paper states no cost or amount for this borrowing.
findings.matters: Q4 liquidity gaps and the use of an overdraft alongside market borrowing show how the council manages its cash-flow low points, which other councils with similar profiles face.
findings.quote: Short term borrowing was required to cover temporary cash flow shortfalls during Q4.

findings.headline: £5.0m of PWLB debt matured in 2025/26 at an average rate of 7.33% and was not replaced with new borrowing, with reserves used to fund borrowing instead.
findings.detail: The council did not replace the maturing debt in-year, consistent with its strategy to maximise use of reserves to initially fund borrowing. The average rate on all debt at 31 March 2026 was 4.38%, and the paper says this average will fall marginally as historic debt leaves the portfolio.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the internal-borrowing choice and the effect on the average cost of debt against their own position.
findings.figures: £5.0m PWLB debt matured; average rate 7.33%; £200.1m total debt at 31 March 2026; average interest rate 4.38%
findings.quote: This historic maturing debt was not replaced with additional in-year new borrowing to maintain the strategy to maximise use of reserves to initially fund borrowing.

findings.headline: East Sussex repaid its last non-PWLB loan, a £6.45m Barclays Market Loan maturing October 2058, early from available balances at a discount to loan value.
findings.detail: The paper reports that no PWLB restructuring took place in the year, but the Barclays Market Loan was repaid early. The saving from the discounted repayment is approximately £0.1m per year, spread over the next 10 years in line with accounting standards.
findings.matters: It removes the council's only remaining non-PWLB debt, and the discounted repayment produces a recurring saving that other councils holding market loans may be weighing.
findings.figures: £6.45m loan; maturity October 2058; approximately £0.1m per year saving over 10 years
findings.quote: The last remaining non-PWLB loan of £6.45m (maturity date October 2058) was repaid early from available balances at an appreciable discount to loan value.

findings.headline: Prior-year bank recommendation for the HSBC foreign payments account was completed, with a new balance sheet code created for it in the general ledger.
findings.detail: The HSBC foreign payments account, holding a trivial balance, was not previously recorded in the general ledger. The fund created code 87102 and set up a reconciliation process, which the auditor confirmed as complete at year-end.
findings.matters: Closing a prior-year control point confirms that the fund has addressed a gap in ledger completeness for a bank account.
findings.figures: 1k balance in the HSBC account (as written in the paper)
findings.quote: Audit team has confirmed as part of their year end procedures that this action has been completed.

findings.headline: Following the Pension Schemes Act 2026, management removed the Virgin Media case from contingent liabilities, but the auditor required disclosure to remain, and management agreed to amend the accounts.
findings.detail: Management said the legislative change means the matter is no longer a contingent liability. The auditor noted some uncertainty remains about applicability to the LGPS and recommended retaining the disclosure.
findings.matters: Other LGPS funds will face the same legislative change, and how the auditor and management reconciled the accounting treatment is directly transferable.
findings.quote: Given the remaining uncertainty, the audit team recommended that appropriate disclosure of this matter be retained within the financial statements.

findings.headline: Pension Fund materiality was set at £78.9 million, up from £63.8 million in the prior year, with performance materiality revised to £55.2 million.
findings.detail: The increase in headline materiality reflects 1.5% of net investment assets at 31 March 2026. Performance materiality was revised because gross investment assets changed significantly from the planning-stage estimate.
