findings.matters: The change shows how a fund's asset base and the audit materiality threshold move together, which affects which misstatements get reported to governance.
findings.figures: £78.9m materiality (prior year £63.8m); £55.2m performance materiality (prior year £47.9m); £3.9m reporting threshold
findings.quote: We have revised the performance materiality due to the actual gross investment assets changing significantly from that anticipated at the planning stage

findings.headline: Audit is substantially complete, and the auditor expects to give an unmodified opinion on the Pension Fund financial statements, but the final opinion awaits the Administering Authority audit.
findings.detail: The Pension Fund Annual Report is not due until 1 December 2026 and has not yet been produced. The auditor will issue the separate Annual Report opinion ahead of completing the audit.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will see the dependency on the Administering Authority audit, which affects when a pension fund opinion can be issued.
findings.quote: we will be unable to issue our final audit opinion on the Pension Fund financial statements until the audit of the Administering Authority is complete.

findings.headline: Auditor reports that the migration of finance data from SAP to Oracle was complete, with no issues noted in accuracy testing.
findings.detail: The auditor tested the reconciliation of balances from SAP onto the Oracle Ledger and used IT audit specialists on the data migration. No matters were raised against this significant risk.
findings.matters: A clean ledger migration is a useful reference point for finance teams at other councils planning or completing a similar system change.
findings.quote: We have reviewed and tested the reconciliation of balances from the SAP system onto the Oracle Ledger and are satisfied that the transfer was complete.

findings.headline: Auditor challenged £445k of reconciling items in the bank reconciliation, which management attributes to the SAP to Oracle migration, and has made a medium-rated recommendation.
findings.detail: Several balances in the listed account codes were not genuine timing differences, making a complete population of reconciling items hard to identify at year-end. The auditor judged the residual difference trivial, and management reports the root cause has been addressed.
findings.matters: Reconciliation problems following a ledger migration are a recognised risk, and other councils moving systems can compare how this one was identified and remediated.
findings.figures: £445k reconciling items; 1 medium-rated recommendation
findings.quote: Within our cash testing, we challenged management regarding the nature of the £445k of reconciling items identified within the bank reconciliation.

findings.headline: Note 26 outstanding capital commitments of £246.2m were found to be inconsistent with supporting workings, which show £220.1m, and management agreed to amend the note.
findings.detail: The auditor identified the difference as an output error in the disclosure. Management confirmed the figure was incorrect and agreed to amend the accounts.
findings.matters: A disclosure error in a capital commitments figure of this size is a point finance officers at other funds and councils would check in their own year-end workings.
findings.figures: £246.2m disclosed; £220.1m independently verified
findings.quote: The disclosure for outstanding capital commitments within Note 26 states a balance of £246.2m.

findings.headline: Auditor identified a £6.2 million understatement of Level 3 investments, which management proposes not to adjust because it is not material.
findings.detail: The understatement arose because investment managers updated valuations after the draft accounts were circulated. Management proposes leaving the accounts unamended, and the Audit Committee will be asked to confirm this through the Letter of Representation.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see how unadjusted valuation timing differences on a £1.15 billion Level 3 portfolio are handled in practice, and how the auditor and management reached the materiality judgement.
findings.figures: £6.2 million understatement; £6,168k net understatement of Level 3 investments; £7,485k understatement in key items; £1.15 billion Level 3 balance; £5,280,556k total net assets per final accounts
findings.quote: This misstatement relates to the valuation of level 3 investments where our testing identified a circa £6.2 million understatement.

findings.headline: The council's SAP system goes out of support in 2027, which the paper treats as a driver of the Oracle timetable
findings.detail: The paper treats the SAP end-of-support date as a driver for the Oracle timetable, and states that the impact of SAP failing would likely be more significant than a poor Oracle go-live.
findings.matters: Legacy ERP end-of-support dates are a common and costly pressure at councils, and the paper's sequencing of this risk against the go-live decision is directly transferable.
findings.quote: The council’s SAP system goes out of support in 2027.

findings.headline: The council estimates that not going live in the October 2026 window would bring significant additional programme and SAP costs in excess of £5 million
findings.detail: The paper sets out the costs of delay, including continued operation of both SAP and Oracle, SAP end-of-life exposure, and the risk of further Oracle updates. The council presents the earliest possible go-live as preferable to this additional cost.
findings.matters: A council's own estimate of the cost of delaying an ERP go-live is the figure a lender or finance director would weigh against the cost of going live with known risks.
findings.figures: in excess of £5 million
findings.quote: Significant additional programme and SAP costs estimated in excess of £5 million.

findings.headline: The Oracle support team has expanded by 5 roles ahead of Phase 3 go-live, and Hypercare documentation has been approved by stakeholders
findings.detail: The 9 October update reports the expansion of the support team and that Hypercare documentation has been created and approved. Recruitment for additional BAU HR and Pay roles is also described in the earlier updates.
findings.matters: Post-go-live support staffing is a recurring cost and capacity question for finance directors budgeting for a new ERP.
findings.figures: 5 roles
findings.quote: The support team have expanded by 5 roles in readiness for Phase 3 go-live

findings.headline: Infosys has added extra resources to its production build and cutover approach at no additional cost to the council
findings.detail: Following a performance review meeting on 10 September 2026, Infosys adopted real-time assurance during cutover and moved smoke testing earlier. The paper says this is achieved with extra Infosys resources at no additional cost.
findings.matters: A supplier absorbing added resource at no cost after a performance escalation is a contract outcome a finance officer elsewhere negotiating with a similar partner would want to know.
findings.quote: This is being achieved with the addition of extra resources by Infosys (at no additional cost)

findings.headline: The Infosys programme lead has resigned and will leave the programme, with other key Infosys roles also lost
findings.detail: The council's implementation partner Infosys has lost its longest-serving programme lead and other key roles, and the paper says the signs are that quality levels are being affected. The council is seeking assurance on leadership cover through go-live.
findings.matters: Loss of supplier leadership during a critical path is a supplier-dependency risk that finance directors at other councils with outsourced implementation partners would recognise.
findings.quote: The Oracle Programme have been informed that the Infosys Programme Lead has resigned and will soon be leaving the programme

findings.headline: 107 known data issues remained open at 9 October 2026, with 49 to be fixed before pay-impacting data migrations from SAP begin on 16 October 2026
findings.detail: The paper describes data migration as much improved but still requiring resolution before the pay-impacting migrations. The 6 November update refers to correcting known production data-migration errors and about 26 known errors carried forward from earlier migration cycles.
findings.matters: Data migration quality is the main determinant of whether a payroll system's first pay run is accurate, and the open count and deadline are concrete markers for a peer council planning a similar move.
findings.figures: 107 known data issues; 49 to be fixed before 16 October 2026; approximately 26 items
findings.quote: There are 107 known data issues to be fixed

findings.headline: Internal audit of payroll readiness, business continuity, access, integration and data migration found no serious control issues preventing a go-live recommendation
findings.detail: The 9 October update says issues were found and will need attention during hypercare, including documentation, tighter governance and process improvements. The paper states that none of the findings were serious control issues that would prevent a go-live recommendation.
findings.matters: Internal audit's view on controls is the assurance a finance director relies on before a payroll system goes live, and the same question arises at other councils.
findings.quote: there were no serious control issues that would prevent a go-live recommendation being made

findings.headline: Phase 3 PPR3 (Run 4) reached 97.64% for ESCC, 93.29% for externals and 97.68% for Fire against a 99% threshold, and the council moved to cutover on a risk-based decision
findings.detail: The 9 October update reports the parallel payroll run results against the 99% threshold and states that all gaps have been accounted for in known issues and data fixes. A risk-based decision was then taken to move into cutover despite the shortfall.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can compare how a council handled a parallel payroll threshold shortfall, and whether it proceeded on a documented risk-based basis.
findings.figures: 97.64% (ESCC); 93.29% (Externals); 97.68% (Fire); threshold 99%
findings.quote: PPR3 (Run 4) reached 97.64% (ESCC), 93.29% (Externals) and 97.68% (Fire) respectively against a threshold of 99%.

findings.headline: Oracle Phase 3 cutover was formally exited on 4 November 2026, with professional users live from that date and the first Oracle payroll on 26 November 2026
findings.detail: The 6 November update records formal exit from cutover, with payroll and other professional users moved first and wider self-service and user roll-out planned around the first payroll date. The 9 October update had described the move to cutover as on time against its stage gate.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council running a similar ERP or payroll migration can see the sequence of gates, the first payroll date and the staged user roll-out the council chose.
findings.figures: 4 Nov 2026; 26 November 2026
findings.quote: Formal exit from Cutover completed.

findings.headline: At the end of Q2, 11 of 11 high-risk audit actions due on a 12-month rolling basis had been confirmed as implemented.
findings.detail: Action tracking seeks written confirmation from services that high-priority actions have been implemented. The report also records 100% implementation of high-priority agreed actions against a 95% target in the performance table.
findings.matters: A finance director can use the implementation rate as a benchmark for how reliably a council is closing audit findings.
findings.figures: 11 of 11 (100%) high-risk actions; target 95% for high-priority agreed actions
findings.quote: As at the end of quarter 2, it was confirmed that 11 of the 11 (100%) high-risk actions due to be implemented on a 12-month rolling basis had been actioned.

findings.headline: IT asset disposal received a reasonable assurance opinion, and management accepted residual risk after the cage access codes were not changed for an extended period.
findings.detail: Disposal processes, the certified disposal partner and CMDB audit trails were found to be appropriate. Two medium-risk findings on an out-of-date disposal contract and the absence of a formal IT asset disposal policy have actions agreed. Shared access codes on padlocked cages are not rotated, and management has accepted the residual risk with no further mitigating controls planned.
findings.matters: A risk accepted by management without further mitigation is a governance decision that finance directors and audit committees elsewhere may want to see explicitly recorded.
findings.quote: However, the access codes have not been changed for an extended period.

findings.headline: Internal Audit planned 54.3% of the audit plan to draft report stage by the end of Q2, against a Q2 target of 45%.
findings.detail: The report also records that six additional audits were added to the plan from contingency and emerging risk days, including IT asset disposal and the Queensway grant, and that two audits were removed.
findings.matters: Finance officers and audit committees elsewhere can compare delivery against the quarterly target and see which emerging-risk areas absorbed contingency time.
findings.figures: 54.3% achieved by the end of Q2; Q2 target 45%
findings.quote: 54.3% achieved by the end of Q2, against a Q2 target of 45%.

findings.headline: Internal Audit found that expenditure on the £2.5m Queensway Gateway Road grant met the grant conditions and that the return to MHCLG was completed correctly.
findings.detail: The Ministry's grant funding agreement required independent assurance, which Internal Audit provided through sample testing and verification of the grant return. A signed declaration was returned within the required timescale.
findings.matters: Councils receiving ringfenced capital grants with independent assurance conditions can see how the requirement was met and that the return was accepted within the deadline.
findings.figures: £2.5m grant from the then Department for Levelling up, Housing and Communities (now MHCLG), provided March 2024
findings.quote: We found that expenditure met the conditions of the grant and that the return submitted to the Ministry had been completed correctly.

findings.headline: The Liquidlogic and ContrOCC adult social care systems, which generated £307 million of payments in 2024/25, received a reasonable assurance opinion.
findings.detail: The audit found access well controlled and payments made correctly and reflected in the accounting system. Actions were agreed on the consistency of debt recovery decisions, the reconciliation of client contributions, defined user access requirements and updated guidance.
findings.matters: The £307 million of payments flowing through these systems is a material share of the council's care spend, so a finance director here or at a peer council would want to know its control environment has been independently tested.
findings.figures: £307 million of payments generated in 2024/25
findings.quote: As a result of our work, we were able to give an opinion of reasonable assurance on the controls in place.

findings.headline: Accounts Receivable in the new Oracle system received a reasonable assurance opinion, the first audit of AR in Oracle.
findings.detail: The audit found appropriate controls over income allocation, unallocated payments and aged debt monitoring. Actions were agreed to configure Oracle to enforce segregation of duties for invoice amendment and cancellation, simplify credit memo matching, and improve reporting.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils completing the same SAP-to-Oracle migration can see which AR control gaps appeared in the first audit after go-live.
findings.quote: As a result of our work, we were able to give an opinion of reasonable assurance.

findings.headline: Procure to Pay in the new Oracle system received a reasonable assurance opinion, the first audit of P2P in Oracle.
findings.detail: The audit found that expenditure is approved with segregation of duties and that payments are made on time. Actions were agreed on raising purchase orders more timeously, aligning approval limits with grades, and developing a report to identify duplicate payments caused by minor data entry errors. No duplicate payments were identified during testing.
findings.matters: Finance officers at councils moving from SAP to Oracle can compare the control points and actions this first post-migration P2P audit raised.
findings.quote: We were, therefore, able to provide an opinion of reasonable assurance.

findings.headline: Internal Audit identified no control weaknesses that would prevent or materially undermine the Oracle HCM and Payroll go-live decision.
findings.detail: Internal Audit completed five pre-go-live assurance reviews covering payroll readiness, security, data migration, integrations and business continuity. No high-risk issues were identified, and a full payroll audit will follow once the system has stabilised.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council planning an ERP or HCM migration can see how one council's assurance programme supported a go-live decision and what it left for post-go-live review.
findings.quote: Based on the assurance work completed, we did not identify any control weaknesses that would prevent or materially undermine a decision to proceed with the Oracle HCM and Payroll go-live.

findings.headline: £445,000 of bank reconciling items arose from the 2025/26 migration from SAP to Oracle, and the council has put in a workaround to strengthen the process.
findings.detail: The paper records one management action on bank reconciliation. It says the reconciling items were not material. It attributes them to Oracle working differently from SAP, and says a workaround has been implemented.
findings.matters: Any council moving finance systems in the same period may meet similar reconciliation gaps when the new system handles transactions differently.
findings.quote: £445,000 of reconciling items were identified relating to the migration from SAP to Oracle during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton reports the Pension Fund audit as substantially complete, with no outstanding matters that would modify the audit opinion.
findings.detail: The paper says the audit is substantially complete at the time of writing. The final opinion on the Fund's financial statements will be issued only after the East Sussex County Council audit is finished later in the year.
findings.matters: A peer or lender can see the audit status and that the opinion depends on the parent council's audit timetable.
findings.quote: The audit of the Fund is substantially complete with no outstanding matters for modification of the audit opinion at the time of writing this report.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton's draft report identifies one valuation misstatement of £6.2m on Level 3 investments, which the paper describes as not material and not adjusted in the accounts.
findings.detail: The paper says the misstatement affects the Net Assets Statement and the Fund Account. The council has decided not to adjust the accounts because it judges the error not material. Some minor disclosure issues were corrected in the accounts.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see that the auditor found a valuation error in the hard-to-price part of the portfolio and that management chose not to adjust it on materiality grounds.
findings.quote: Whilst the report identifies one misstatement that impacts on the Net Assets Statement and the Fund Account, through the valuation of Level 3 investments, at £6.2m, the error is not material and, therefore, does not require an adjustment to the accounts.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton recommends corporate oversight of key contracts under the new sovereign procurement function, alongside embedding the refreshed contract management framework.
findings.detail: This improvement recommendation under Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness asks the Council to continue embedding the refreshed contract management framework and playbook, and to set up corporate oversight of key contracts. Management response says a new SharePoint site will be developed during 2027 and that new Oracle functionality will provide improved oversight of contract data.
findings.matters: Councils reorganising procurement into a central function can compare how this council is building contract oversight and the timetable it has set for doing so.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Establish arrangements for corporate oversight of key contracts to support consistent oversight and timely action.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton recommends governance and monitoring for the local SEND Reform Plan to mitigate the 'growing DSG deficit'.
findings.detail: This improvement recommendation under Financial Sustainability asks for established governance and oversight of the SEND Reform Plan, and for robust monitoring with regular reporting to members on forecasts, emerging risks and mitigations. Management response states that governance and monitoring are established and operating through the ESCC SEND Reform Plan and the Department of Education's SEND Reform monitoring framework.
findings.matters: A growing high-needs DSG deficit driven by SEND is a pressure many councils face, and the paper shows one council's governance response to it.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Established governance and oversight arrangements to support effective delivery of the local SEND Reform Plan to ensure that the growing DSG deficit is mitigated.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton rates Governance arrangements green and Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness amber for 2025/26, and reports no significant weaknesses in the Council's response to its financial challenges.
findings.detail: The report notes GT has identified no significant weaknesses in the Council's response to its financial challenges. Governance is rated green and Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness amber. Financial Sustainability remains the only area rated red.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils can compare these ratings with their own, particularly the split between a red financial sustainability rating and green governance.
findings.figures: Ratings: Financial Sustainability red; Governance green; Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness amber. The report contains one key and two improvement recommendations.
findings.quote: with a green rating in terms of Governance arrangements and an amber rating for Improving Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness.

findings.headline: East Sussex has required Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for its 2026/27 revenue budget, and current projections indicate EFS will also be needed for 2027/28.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton rates Financial Sustainability 'red'. Its key recommendation asks the Council to reduce reliance on EFS over time and to report transparently to members on the expected EFS level, the drivers, and the actions taken. Management response says all efforts will be made to set a robust budget within the context of continuing EFS, and that engagement with MHCLG and lobbying will continue.
findings.matters: A council that needs EFS for two consecutive budget years, with the second already projected, is a direct reference point for other councils and lenders assessing how long government support may last.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Given the Council has required Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to support its 2026/27 revenue budget

findings.headline: All 8 treasury management prudential indicators are reported as compliant for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council is required to report actual prudential indicators after each year-end. It says the eight treasury indicators in Appendix 4 show the council is fully compliant.
findings.matters: A clean compliance result against the prudential indicators is the basis finance directors and auditors use to judge borrowing controls.
findings.figures: 8 treasury management indicators
findings.quote: demonstrating that the Council is fully compliant with these indicators

findings.headline: Long-term debt was £194.6m at 30 September 2026, with an average rate of 4.30%, against £200.1m and 4.38% at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The paper gives the average rate of all debt at 31 March 2026 as 4.38%. The fall in debt over the half-year reflects the PWLB maturities reported in the paper.
findings.matters: A falling debt stock with a falling average rate shows the direction of the council's borrowing cost, which is what lenders and peers track.
findings.figures: £194.6m at 30 September 2026; 4.30% average rate; £200.1m and 4.38% at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: was £194.6m held at an average rate of 4.30%

findings.headline: Two PWLB loans totalling £5.5m at an average rate of 7.125% matured in the first half of 2026/27, and no new PWLB borrowing was taken.
findings.detail: The paper says no further PWLB maturities are due in 2026/27. Long-term debt at 30 September 2026 was £194.6m at an average rate of 4.30%.
findings.matters: Maturing high-rate PWLB debt that is not replaced with new PWLB borrowing changes both the council's debt cost and its refinancing exposure.
findings.figures: £5.5m matured; average rate 7.125%; no new PWLB borrowing; long-term debt £194.6m; average rate 4.30%
findings.quote: Two loans matured totalling £5.5m at an average rate of 7.125%

findings.headline: Investment interest for the six months to 30 September 2026 averaged 3.95%, above the SONIA benchmark of 3.73%.
findings.detail: The paper reports £0.9m of short-term interest received over the six months. For 2025/26 it reported £4.5m at an average rate of 4.51%, against a SONIA benchmark of 4.04%.
findings.matters: Earning above the benchmark while balances are shrinking is useful evidence for finance directors comparing returns with peer authorities.
findings.figures: £0.9m interest received; average rate 3.95%; SONIA benchmark 3.73%; 2025/26: £4.5m at 4.51% against SONIA 4.04%
findings.quote: This was above the benchmark of SONIA in the same period of 3.73%.

findings.headline: Fixed-term deposits totalling £22m were placed in the first half of 2026/27 at rates between 3.97% and 4.25%.
findings.detail: The paper says these deposits secure a fixed rate of return for up to three months, which it presents as earning more than overnight balances in money market funds.
findings.matters: The rates achieved on fixed-term deposits show the return the council is earning on the cash it still holds.
findings.figures: £22m placed; rates between 3.97% and 4.25%
findings.quote: fixed term deposits totalling £22m were placed at rates between 3.97% and 4.25%

findings.headline: Fixed-term deposits were £12.2m at 30 September 2026, down from £71.8m a year earlier.
findings.detail: The paper says fewer fixed-term deposits were placed because investment balances had fallen. Fixed-term deposits are used to lock in returns for up to three months.
findings.matters: A fall in deposits this size shows how far cash balances have dropped and reduces the council's ability to earn returns on fixed terms.
findings.figures: £12.2m at 30 September 2026; £71.8m at September 2025; reduction of £59.6m
findings.quote: was placed on deposit (September 2025, £71.8m) a reduction of £59.6m over the year

findings.headline: The 2026/27 treasury strategy was prepared around £70m of Exceptional Financial Support, which the paper describes as a capitalisation direction financed through borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper says the EFS does not provide additional funding but allows revenue expenditure to be financed through borrowing, which raises the council's borrowing requirement and financing costs.
findings.matters: A council using a capitalisation direction to fund revenue spending through borrowing is a key structural point for any finance director and for lenders assessing the council's debt.
findings.figures: £70m Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27
findings.quote: EFS does not provide additional funding but instead provides a capitalisation direction that allows revenue expenditure to be financed through borrowing.

findings.headline: Investment balances fell to £30.4m at 31 March 2026 from £115.3m at 31 March 2025.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall to the planned use of reserves, increased creditor payments and debt maturities. Short-term borrowing from other local authorities and an agreed bank overdraft were used to cover cash shortfalls from December 2025 to March 2026.
findings.matters: Cash balances falling to this level and the need for short-term borrowing to cover shortfalls are signs of a liquidity position that finance directors and lenders watch closely.
findings.figures: £30.4m at 31 March 2026; £115.3m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: were utilised to cover temporary cash flow shortfalls between December 2025 and March 2026

findings.headline: A Barclays Market Loan of £6.45m, maturing October 2058, was repaid early at a discount to loan value in Q1 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the loan was the last remaining non-PWLB loan and was repaid from available balances with help from the council's treasury advisors, MUFG. The paper says the saving will be spread over 10 years under accounting standards.
findings.matters: A finance director, or a lender to the council, can see that a non-PWLB market loan has ended before maturity and how the saving is being recognised.
findings.figures: £6.45m loan; maturity October 2058; savings of approximately £0.1m per year over 10 years
findings.quote: Savings from the discounted repayment of approximately £0.1m per year will be spread over the next 10 years in line with accounting standards.

findings.headline: Q2 final audit reports were below the historical quarterly average because audit resources moved to the Oracle HCM and Payroll implementation.
findings.detail: The report describes the lower number of final reports as a planned variance caused by increased deployment of audit resources to the imminent implementation of the Oracle Human Capital Management and Payroll system. The team prioritised advisory and control assurance work during the transition.
findings.matters: A council or finance team planning a payroll or HCM system go-live can see how one authority's internal audit capacity was reallocated during implementation.
findings.quote: increased deployment of audit resources to the imminent implementation of the Oracle Human Capital Management (HCM) and Payroll system

findings.headline: 11 of 11 (100%) high-risk audit improvement actions due for implementation on the 12-month rolling basis were confirmed as actioned by the end of Q2.
findings.detail: Internal Audit obtains written confirmation from services that high-priority actions agreed with management and due for implementation are complete. At the end of Q2 all 11 due actions were confirmed as actioned.
findings.matters: Follow-through on high-risk audit actions is a measure a finance director can use to judge whether control weaknesses are being closed rather than carried forward.
findings.figures: 11 of 11 actions (100%)
findings.quote: 11 of the 11 (100%) high-risk actions due to be implemented on a 12-month rolling basis had been actioned

findings.headline: All 5 audits finalised in Q2 with a formal opinion received reasonable assurance, with no partial or minimal opinions.
findings.detail: The report states that all five audits finalised in the quarter with a formal audit opinion received reasonable assurance. It also records that no partial or minimal assurance opinions were given.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can use this as a comparison point for the assurance outcomes of a similar internal audit programme in the same period.
findings.figures: 5 audits; 0 partial or minimal assurance opinions
findings.quote: all received opinions of reasonable assurance. There were no partial or minimal assurance opinions.

findings.headline: Backing for gross internal area and land area records still unresolved, first raised in 2023/24
findings.detail: The council was unable or struggled to obtain backing for some gross internal area and land area records. The issue was first raised in 2023/24, and the council says a project to remeasure GIAs is ongoing. Management will continue to review documentation and obtain support where needed.
findings.matters: A recurring audit point on asset records is one that persists across years and that peer councils with large property estates may also carry.
findings.quote: This issue still persists, having been raised in 2023/24, with the Council stating there is an ongoing project to remeasure GIAs.

findings.headline: Council does not perform a formal group boundary assessment
findings.detail: Group boundary judgements made when arrangements are set up are carried forward, with no documented process to reassess them. GT warns this could miss new subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures and lead to non-compliance with the CIPFA Code. Management says it does not believe there is a current risk and will put a process in place.
findings.matters: Whether a council's group accounts are complete depends on this assessment, and it is relevant to any council with companies, trusts or partnerships.
findings.quote: The Council does not perform a formal group boundary assessment.

findings.headline: 4 out of 49 Councillors did not return a signed year-end register of interests declaration
findings.detail: Four councillors did not provide a signed year-end declaration. The paper says multiple attempts were made to get the information from councillors who did not return after the May 2026 elections. GT recommends stronger controls so that all councillors complete the register.
findings.matters: Incomplete related-party disclosures are a recurring audit finding, and the election-year cause is one other councils may face.
findings.figures: 4 out of 49 Councillors
findings.quote: 4 out of 49 Councillors did not provide a signed year-end register of interests declaration form.

findings.headline: Manual journals below £1m can be posted without formal review or authorisation in Oracle
findings.detail: The Oracle general ledger allows individuals to post manual journals under a £1m threshold without formal review. GT raised this as a best-practice recommendation to reassess the threshold or add proportionate independent review. Management says current controls would detect material errors, and it will keep the threshold under review, noting that lower limits add administrative burden.
findings.matters: Journal authorisation thresholds are a standard control that other councils and external auditors compare, and a £1m threshold is a specific, comparable figure.
findings.quote: There is currently a £1m threshold for which individuals may post manual journals, without having to receive formal review or authorisation within the Oracle general ledger system.

findings.headline: Monthly bank reconciliation report has no formal review or sign-off process
findings.detail: The Income Allocation Team produces a monthly bank reconciliation report after period close, but there is no formal review or sign-off. GT recommends a documented sign-off. Management says daily reconciliations are already done and agrees to add monthly sign-off from the Financial Accounting Team.
findings.matters: Without named accountability for the monthly report, errors can go undetected, which is a control point most finance directors would check.
findings.quote: Currently, the Income Allocation Team produces a monthly report following period close, however, there is no formal review and sign off process.

findings.headline: Sample testing found year-end creditors balances overstated through administrative errors
findings.detail: GT's sample testing found a number of year-end creditors balances were overstated. Management attributes this to administrative errors, has reviewed the two items extrapolated, and says the errors were isolated rather than a systemic control weakness. A formal review of the creditors process is under way.
findings.matters: Year-end cut-off and creditor accuracy affect the reported position at the balance sheet date, and the council's view that the errors were isolated is one a peer or lender may want to test.
findings.quote: Sample testing of year-end creditors balances identified a number of instances whereby the creditors balance was overstated at the year end.

findings.headline: Council unable to provide workings behind the impaired debt provision percentages
findings.detail: The percentages used in the impaired debt provision came from analysis made when the methodology was first developed, some years ago. The council could not provide the supporting workings, so GT flagged a risk that the provision is not supported or reflects current recovery experience. Management will review the percentages annually and share workings with the auditors.
findings.matters: An unsupported bad-debt provision can misstate debtors and reserves, and it is a common audit point for councils with large sundry debt books.
findings.quote: The council was unable to provide the supporting workings and documentation evidencing how these percentages were originally calculated.

findings.headline: £61.249m Social Care Grant reclassified from non-specific to specific in the audited accounts
findings.detail: The draft accounts treated the grant as non-specific and non-ring-fenced. GT assessed it as specific to adult and children's social care, and the council has adjusted 2024/25 and 2025/26 accordingly. The paper says these adjustments do not change the reported deficit or reserves position.
findings.matters: Grant classification affects how income is presented and how much flexibility a council has over it, and other councils treating similar grants may face the same question.
findings.quote: which had been treated in the draft statement of accounts as non-specific/non-ring fenced

findings.headline: GT is anticipating an unqualified audit opinion on East Sussex's 2025/26 Statement of Accounts
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer reports that GT expects to issue an unqualified opinion. The audit report says final audit file review and a review of the final financial statements remain outstanding, but it states there is no suggestion this will require the opinion or statement of accounts to change.
findings.matters: A clean opinion on 2025/26 is the outcome a lender or peer finance team checks first, and the paper states the conditions under which it is expected to hold.
findings.quote: GT is anticipating being able to issue an unqualified audit opinion for the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts.

findings.headline: The Subgroup has increased its meeting frequency ahead of the Phase 3 go-live date.
findings.detail: The Subgroup met on 11 September, 9 October, 22 October and 6 November 2026. The paper links the increased frequency to the proximity of the Phase 3 go-live.
findings.matters: Oversight intensity around a go-live is a governance choice other councils can compare when setting their own programme assurance.
findings.figures: Meetings on 11 September, 9 October, 22 October and 6 November 2026.
findings.quote: The Subgroup has increased its frequency of meetings given the proximity of the planned go-live date for the final phase (Phase 3) of the Oracle implementation.

findings.headline: The paper lists build quality, resourcing and data migration as risks that remain within the Oracle implementation.
findings.detail: The paper says the remaining risks were weighed against the risks of not going live, which it describes as materially greater. It also says the programme cannot entirely mitigate every potential issue, and that it would not be cost-effective to try.
findings.matters: Naming the specific residual risks at go-live gives a peer council a checklist to test its own ERP readiness against.
findings.figures: None stated.
findings.quote: Whilst risks remain within the implementation (such as build quality, resourcing and data migration), it is not possible (nor cost -effective) for the programme to entirely mitigate against potential issues or risks materialising.

findings.headline: The Subgroup records a lack of Internal Audit material concerns about going live with Phase 3.
findings.detail: The Subgroup's most recent meetings noted that Internal Audit has no material concerns about going live. The paper presents this as a position reached in the Subgroup's review.
findings.matters: Internal audit's view before a major financial system go-live is a control assurance point that finance directors and external auditors look for in peer implementations.
findings.figures: None stated.
findings.quote: The lack of Internal Audit material concerns to going live;

findings.headline: East Sussex reports its Oracle HR and Payroll go-live, including the first payroll run in Oracle, as on track for November 2026.
findings.detail: The Subgroup's 6 November meeting received a status update that the planned November go-live remained on track. Professional users are already processing the November payroll in the live system, and all users are due to have access from 26 November.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council running an ERP replacement can compare this go-live date and sequencing with their own plan.
findings.figures: All users access Oracle from 26 November; payslips due 23 or 24 November. No monetary figures in the paper.
findings.quote: The planned November go -live for HR and Payroll, including running the first payroll in Oracle in November, remained on track.

findings.headline: East Sussex County Council will cease to exist and merge with five borough and district councils in 2028, under the 'One East Sussex' local government reform.
findings.detail: The paper says the Government has adopted the 'One East Sussex' proposals and that the county council will be replaced by one strategic authority. The Fund plans to address the effects on its employers, assets and liabilities.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council going through local government reform can compare how a pension fund is preparing for the merger of its administering authority.
findings.figures: five borough and district councils; 2028
findings.quote: This means that East Sussex County Council (the administering authority for the LGPS in the geographical area of East Sussex) will cease to exist, merging with the five borough and district councils that are currently in place in the county.

findings.headline: The paper says the legislation makes clear that the Council's Section 151 Officer cannot be the Senior LGPS Officer.
findings.detail: The Senior LGPS Officer role must be adopted by the Fund by 31 December 2026. The paper says clear boundaries between the two roles are needed, and the arrangements are ongoing.
findings.matters: A council's finance director cannot also fill the statutory Senior LGPS Officer role, so the council will need a separate appointment.
findings.figures: 31 December 2026 deadline
findings.quote: The legislation and accompanying guidance make it clear that the Council’s Section 151 Officer cannot be the Senior LGPS Officer

findings.headline: The Fund is advertising for an Independent Person ahead of the 31 December 2026 deadline for the Fit for the Future governance requirements.
findings.detail: The paper says the Fund must adopt a Senior LGPS Officer by 31 December 2026 and that the Section 151 Officer cannot take that role. Recruitment for the Independent Person has started, and plans for the Senior LGPS Officer are described as underway.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will need to know that the statutory Senior LGPS Officer role cannot sit with the Section 151 Officer.
findings.figures: 31 December 2026 deadline
findings.quote: appoint an Independent Person and are now advertising for the role well ahead of the 31st December 2026 deadline.

findings.headline: The Pension Committee put a hold on material investment strategy changes, delaying illiquid asset allocations to return to benchmark weights.
findings.detail: The paper links the hold to uncertainty around investment pooling. The delay affects parts of the illiquid asset portfolio that were below target weights.
findings.matters: Delayed allocations to illiquid assets show how pooling uncertainty can push back investment plans at other funds going through the same transition.
findings.quote: The Pension Committee put on hold any material changes to investment strategy to take account of the uncertainty around investment pooling, most notably delaying allocation to parts of the illiquid asset portfolio to bring the Fund back up to targeted benchmark weights.

findings.headline: The Fund expects to become increasingly cashflow negative as employer contribution rates fall and pension increases have been high.
findings.detail: The paper says the Fund is already cashflow negative from member activities. It says the reduction in employer contributions and the high inflation uplift on pensions in payment will increase this, and the Committee will focus on income in future strategy.
findings.matters: A fund moving from positive to negative cashflow must sell or draw on investments to pay pensions, which affects how the council's other funding and borrowing decisions are viewed.
findings.figures: Pension increases for the year were 1.7%, down from 6.7% and 10.1% in the preceding two years.
findings.quote: the reduction in employer contribution rates will mean that the Fund will become increasingly cashflow negative in the coming years.

findings.headline: The Fund reaffirmed a funding level of 117% at the 31 March 2025 triennial valuation, and most employers' contribution rates fell.
findings.detail: The paper reports the outcome of the triennial valuation and notes that the majority of employers saw a fall in contribution rates. It describes the Fund as very strong on assets against liabilities.
findings.matters: A funding level above 100% and falling employer contributions are the measures a finance director at another council would compare against their own pension deficit or surplus.
findings.figures: 117% funding level at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Fund re-affirmed a strong funding level of 117% as at 31March 2025 and the majority of the Fund’s employers saw a fall in contribution rates.

findings.headline: The Fund joined the Border to Coast Pension Partnership pool on 1 April 2026, with the ACCESS pool being wound down.
findings.detail: The Fund was required to change pools after government did not support ACCESS's proposal. At 31 March 2026, most of the Fund's assets were still held in ACCESS pooled funds, and the transfer is expected to take some months.
findings.matters: Councils and lenders watching the LGPS pooling reforms can see how a fund moved pools and how much of its assets had to be transferred.
findings.figures: £5.3bn total Fund assets; £3.6bn invested in pooled funds with ACCESS
findings.quote: As at 31st March 2026 the total value of the Fund’s assets was £5.3bn of which £3.6bn was invested in pooled funds with ACCESS.

findings.headline: The Fund returned 6.1% in the year to 31 March 2026, with an underperformance of 4.5% against its benchmark.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the shortfall to growth, quality and sustainability-oriented equity strategies, rising bond yields and inflation, and ESG mandates constrained by sector exclusions. The paper says the long-term strategy is unchanged.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size of a benchmark shortfall in a single year with the causes the Fund gives for it.
findings.figures: 6.1%; underperformance of 4.5%
findings.quote: The investment return for the year to 31 March 2026 was a positive 6.1%, however when compared to the benchmark, this was an underperformance of 4.5%.

findings.headline: Estimated lithium extraction exposure is £12.3m (0.2% of the Fund), falling to approximately £0.8m (0.02%) once adjusted for the share of company revenue from lithium
findings.detail: Following a September 2026 committee request, officers identified the Fund's holdings in companies with exposure to lithium extraction. Adjusting for the proportion of company revenues attributable to lithium extraction reduces the estimated exposure substantially.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council responding to similar questions can see how the choice of exposure measure (gross holding versus revenue-adjusted) changes the reported figure by more than an order of magnitude.
findings.figures: Gross exposure £12.3 million (0.2% of the Fund); revenue-adjusted exposure approximately £0.8 million (0.02% of the Fund)
findings.quote: reduces the estimated exposure to approximately £0.8 million, equivalent to 0.02% of the Fund.

findings.headline: BCPP will not implement the index-linked gilt trigger framework until the Fund onboards to its Investment Management Services from 1 April 2027
findings.detail: BCPP is receptive to the proposed trigger framework but says it lacks some asset data feeds, trading capability, full trading authority and the ability to monitor the framework's risks until onboarding. It considers it would be inappropriate to implement the trigger before the Fund is fully onboarded.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can see a pool-led strategy change being held until operational onboarding is complete, which affects when a council's implementation timetable can be met.
findings.figures: IMS onboarding expected from 1 April 2027
findings.quote: BCPP therefore considers that it would be inappropriate for it to assume responsibility for implementing a trigger mechanism before the Fund has been fully onboarded to IMS.

findings.headline: Fund joined Border to Coast Pensions Partnership on 1 April 2026 after the Government did not support continuation of the ACCESS pool
findings.detail: The report says the Fund's previous pool, ACCESS, would not continue under the new pooling arrangements. The Fund remains responsible for setting its investment objectives and Strategic Asset Allocation, while BCPP will increasingly implement the agreed strategy. Transfers of investments into BCPP pooled equity and real estate funds took place during the quarter.
findings.matters: Any council moving its pension investments into a new pool under the same government timetable faces the same split of responsibilities between administering authority and pool.
findings.figures: Joined BCPP 1 April 2026
findings.quote: The Fund joined Border to Coast Pensions Partnership (BCPP) on 1 April 2026 following the Government's decision not to support the continuation of the Fund's previous LGPS Pool, ACCESS, under the new pooling arrangements.

findings.headline: Private credit is around 3% below its strategic allocation, and illiquid assets are 22.1% of the Fund against a 26.5% strategic allocation
findings.detail: The report describes the main allocation gap as private credit, expected to narrow as existing commitments are drawn down. The illiquid share of assets is below its strategic level, and the Fund's 30% illiquid-asset ceiling would only be exceeded if liquid assets fell by approximately 35%.
findings.matters: A lender or finance officer can see the Fund's liquidity headroom against its own illiquid-asset limit, and how far its private market commitments have yet to be drawn.
findings.figures: Private credit approximately 3% below strategic allocation; actual illiquid 22.1% vs strategic 26.5%; actual liquid 78.0% vs strategic 73.5%; illiquid ceiling 30%; liquid fall before ceiling approximately 35%
findings.quote: The main difference continues to be private credit, which remains around 3% below its strategic allocation.

findings.headline: Investment income of £74.37m received to 30 September 2026 against a full-year forecast of £176.27m
findings.detail: The forecast assumes a further £101.90m of investment income will be received in the second half of 2026/27, which is over half of the full-year figure. The report notes that the annual comparison alone does not establish the cash available at each payment date.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can see how heavily a pension fund's cash plan depends on second-half investment income arriving as forecast.
findings.figures: Income received £74.37m; full-year forecast £176.27m; remaining H2 assumption £101.90m
findings.quote: Investment income received to 30 September 2026 totalled £74.37m, against a full-year forecast of £176.27m.

findings.headline: Forecast 2026/27 net cash outflow is £59.95m, up £3.81m from the original £56.14m, driven by higher payments
findings.detail: Forecast payments rose £7.26m to £239.02m, including £4.84m more non-payroll benefit payments and £2.54m more pensioner payroll. Forecast receipts rose £3.45m to £179.07m, mainly from higher contributions after a larger pay award and new employers joining. The report states the increase does not represent a funding deficit, and the custodian cash account held £102.72m at 30 September 2026.
findings.matters: Rising benefit payments against a growing cash outflow show how a pension fund's liquidity needs move with pay awards and employer admissions, and the report says non-payroll payments are hard to forecast.
findings.figures: Net outflow £59.95m (original £56.14m, change £3.81m); payments £239.02m (original £231.76m, change £7.26m); receipts £179.07m (original £175.62m, change £3.45m); non-payroll benefit payments up £4.84m to £62.54m; custodian cash £102.72m
findings.quote: This is £3.81m higher than the original forecast outflow of £56.14m and represents the amount to be met through investment income and transfers from the custodian cash account.

findings.headline: Fund returned 0.2% in the quarter to 30 September 2026, against a strategic benchmark return of 0.9%
findings.detail: The Fund was valued at approximately £5.55 billion at 30 September 2026. The report says performance remained below benchmark over the longer term, by 4.2% over one year and 3.8% per annum over three years. Public equities were below benchmark, and infrastructure and property were weaker within private markets.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see the size of the gap between the Fund's return and its benchmark over one, three and one quarter, which bears on the Fund's funding position.
findings.figures: Fund value approximately £5.55 billion; Q3 return 0.2%; benchmark return 0.9%; one-year shortfall 4.2%; three-year shortfall 3.8% per annum
findings.quote: The Fund returned 0.2% during the quarter, compared with its strategic benchmark return of 0.9%.

findings.headline: One employer remains to be onboarded to i-Connect, with the Fund working to finish before the next Annual Benefit Statement cycle.
findings.detail: The Fund is holding fortnightly progress calls with the employer and its new payroll software provider. Officers are also tracking payroll changes such as Oracle for East Sussex County Council, academy conversions, and TUPE transfers that affect i-Connect data readiness.
findings.matters: Data feeds from employers to the pension fund determine how accurate and timely member records are, and payroll-system changes are a common source of delay for other funds.
findings.figures: 1 employer remaining to be onboarded
findings.quote: Only one employer remains to be on-boarded

findings.headline: Officers standardised 5,577 deferred member addresses into Royal Mail format and updated 673 traced addresses with a high conviction of accuracy.
findings.detail: The LexisNexis data service provided under the Heywood Altair contract was used for the address tracing upload. Medium-conviction addresses are being double-checked, and the reliability of name, date of birth, email, and phone data is still being assessed.
findings.matters: Deferred member tracing affects how many members can be reached for benefit payments and reduces the risk of unpaid or misdirected benefits, which other funds are also working to address.
findings.figures: 5,577 addresses standardised; 673 addresses updated

findings.headline: All 58 in-scope 2025/26 Annual Allowance cases had calculations and letters issued before the 6 October 2026 statutory deadline.

findings.headline: Government has adopted the 'One East Sussex' proposals, with East Sussex County Council to cease to exist and merge with the five borough and district councils, and one strategic authority coming into being in 2028
findings.detail: The paper says the administering authority for the LGPS in East Sussex will be replaced by one strategic authority. It lists merging notional assets and liabilities of the defunct councils among the changes the fund must respond to.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation that abolishes a county council and its pension fund's administering authority is a structural change that finance directors and lenders in other areas will watch.

findings.headline: Fund must adopt a Senior LGPS Officer role by 31 December 2026, which the Section 151 Officer cannot hold
findings.detail: Fit for the Future legislation created the role, which will be responsible for all aspects of managing the LGPS within the administering authority. The paper says arrangements to separate it from the Section 151 Officer role are ongoing.
findings.matters: The requirement that a council's section 151 officer cannot also run the pension fund affects how finance directors allocate responsibilities, and the deadline is one other councils must also meet.

findings.detail: The Pension Committee paused material strategy changes because of uncertainty around pooling. The delay means the fund has not yet brought illiquid asset holdings back up to target benchmark weights.
findings.matters: Delayed rebalancing into illiquid assets shows how pooling transition can hold back planned allocations, a pressure other funds in the same position may face.

findings.detail: The paper reports that the government did not support the ACCESS pool's proposal, so the fund moved to Border to Coast Pension Partnership. Wind-down of ACCESS will take some time, with the priority being the safe and efficient transfer of assets.
findings.matters: Pool transitions of this size move billions of pension assets between structures and carry transfer and wind-down risk, which other funds and lenders to councils will track as the pool landscape changes.

findings.headline: Fund expects to become increasingly cashflow negative in coming years as employer contribution rates fall and pensions in payment rise
findings.detail: The paper says the fund was already cashflow negative from member activities. It links the expected worsening to lower employer contribution rates and the high inflation uplift applied to pensions in payment in recent years. It says the fund will focus on income when setting strategy.
findings.matters: A pension fund moving to sustained cashflow deficit changes how it funds benefit payments from investment income and assets, which is relevant to councils treating the fund as a long-term funding source.

findings.quote: the reduction in employer contribution rates will mean that the Fund will become increasingly cashflow negative in the coming years.

findings.detail: The triennial valuation was completed over the year and an updated Funding Strategy Statement was to be in place by 31 March 2026. The paper says the majority of employers saw a fall in contribution rates.
findings.matters: Employer contribution rates set by the valuation determine the cash the fund receives from every participating council, which matters to finance directors budgeting employer costs.

findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can compare this shortfall with their own pension exposure and the investment assumptions behind their contribution rates.

findings.headline: The auditor reports that the migration of fund ledger balances from SAP to Oracle was complete and that no accuracy issues were found in the transferred data.
findings.detail: Key finance data moved from SAP to Oracle at the start of 2025/26, and all year transactions were recorded on Oracle. The auditor's IT specialists assisted with the data migration testing, and the auditor carried out completeness and accuracy reconciliations between the two systems.
findings.matters: The auditor's conclusion on a ledger migration is a reference point for finance teams at other councils planning or running the same kind of system change.
findings.quote: We have reviewed and tested the reconciliation of balances from the SAP system onto the Oracle Ledger and are satisfied that the transfer was complete.

findings.headline: The auditor raised a medium-rated recommendation on £445k of reconciling items in the bank reconciliation, which management links to the SAP-to-Oracle migration.
findings.detail: The auditor could not readily identify a complete population of genuine reconciling items at year end, because several balances in the listed account codes were not genuine timing differences. The auditor judged the residual difference trivial, and management reports a root cause fix and a dedicated reconciliation process for account 87104.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council moving ledgers would want to see how reconciliation controls were affected by a system change, including manual intervention on payments processed through Altair.
findings.figures: £445k reconciling items; Medium rating
findings.quote: Within our cash testing, we challenged management regarding the nature of the £445k of reconciling items identified within the bank reconciliation.

findings.detail: The auditor found the disclosed figure was an output error inconsistent with the supporting workings. The auditor treated the difference as non-trivial and recommended the note be updated, and management agreed.
findings.matters: A disclosed commitment figure overstated by about £26m is a reporting error that finance teams and lenders reading pension fund commitments would want to see corrected.

findings.quote: The disclosure for outstanding capital commitments within Note 26 states a balance of £246.2m.

findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know that unadjusted Level 3 valuation differences are being carried in the accounts, and that the auditor treats the cause as common across LGPS funds.

findings.detail: The council is deliberately using internal cash reserves rather than incurring new debt during a period of high interest rates. This represents a strategic choice to manage borrowing costs, but indicates that liquid financial resources are declining significantly. The paper notes the council has £75.000m of internal borrowing (reserves) available to support 2026/27 capital spending, with new external borrowing expected to fund the remainder.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial resilience would be concerned about the rapid depletion of liquid reserves, while peer finance directors would track this as a response to rate pressure and question whether this rate of reserve use is sustainable.
findings.figures: Opening cash £137.2m (Q1 2025/26), closing £65.5m (Q1 2026/27); 52% reduction
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 30 June 2026 have fallen by 52% in one year, from £137.2m at Q1 2025/26 to £65.5m due to continued use of cash balances to support the capital programme and revenue cashflow requirements whilst new borrowing is delayed during a time of elevated rates.

findings.headline: Investment management is delivering above-benchmark returns despite cash position constraints, demonstrating competent treasury execution under stress.
findings.detail: Q1 average investment return of 4.01% exceeded the SONIA benchmark of 3.73% by 28 basis points. Investment risk exposure (0.004–0.005%) remains far below the strategy's allowable limit of 0.050%, indicating disciplined credit quality management. This performance is achieved while managing a falling and constrained portfolio.
findings.matters: Strong treasury management during a period of cash depletion and liquidity pressure demonstrates financial discipline and capability, which supports lender confidence in the council's ability to manage large external borrowing programmes.
findings.figures: Investment return 4.01% vs 3.73% SONIA (+28 basis points); investment risk 0.004–0.005% vs 0.050% limit
findings.quote: The average investment return over Q1 was 4.01% performing above the benchmark rate by 28 basis points (or 0.28 percentage points).

findings.headline: Council expects to require £136.558m in new external borrowing during 2026/27, to be raised after exhausting £75.000m of internal resources.
findings.detail: The strategy allocates £75.000m of internal borrowing (reserves and temporary working capital) towards the capital and capitalisation programmes. This leaves £136.558m that must be raised from external debt markets. The timing of this borrowing will be managed in relation to treasury strategy and economic conditions.
findings.matters: A borrowing requirement of this scale and imminence will determine the council's market access and cost of capital, directly affecting whether it can proceed with capital plans; the wording about timing suggests borrowing may be deferred if rates remain high.
findings.figures: £136.558m new external borrowing; £75.000m internal borrowing; £211.558m total 2026/27 borrowing requirement
findings.quote: It is therefore expected that new borrowing of £136.558m may be required to support the capital programme and capitalisation direction during 2026/27, although the timing of actual borrowing will be considered in the context of the wider treasury management position and underlying economic environment.

findings.headline: Capital programme costs have increased above original forecast, raising total external borrowing requirement by £2.136m to £211.558m.
findings.detail: Capital programme CFR closing balance revised upward from £334.064m to £339.700m. Capital programme borrowing requirement increased from £30.008m original estimate to £33.344m revised forecast. Total new borrowing requirement now £211.558m against original estimate of £209.422m.
findings.matters: Cost overruns mean larger funding gaps; combined with depleting cash reserves, the council has less flexibility to absorb further programme pressures or delays in accessing debt markets.
findings.figures: Capital programme CFR £334.064m to £339.700m; capital borrowing requirement £30.008m to £33.344m; total borrowing need £211.558m vs £209.422m forecast
findings.quote: The total CFR is expected to give rise to a new borrowing requirement of £211.558m (£141.558m capital programme and £70.000m capitalisation direction) by the end of the year, compared to the original estimate of requirement of £209.422m (£139.422m capital programme and £70.000m capitalisation direction).

findings.headline: Cash investment balances have fallen 52% in one year to £65.5m as the council uses reserves to fund capital and revenue spending while delaying new borrowing.
findings.detail: Balances fell from £137.2m in Q1 2025/26 to £65.5m in Q1 2026/27. The council is using cash reserves to support capital programme and revenue spending rather than accessing debt markets, a deliberate strategy given current interest rates. A £2.0m PWLB loan at 7.125% matured during the quarter.
findings.matters: Rapidly shrinking liquidity cushion means the council will be forced to enter debt markets for substantial sums within months, reducing flexibility to time borrowing decisions or manage market windows.
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 30 June 2026 have fallen by 52% in one year, from £137.2m at Q1 2025/26 to £65.5m due to continued use of cash balances to support the capital programme and revenue cashflow requirements whilst new borrowing is delayed during a time of elevated rates.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report PTBs and ITT
findings.headline: Uptake of the council's cost-mitigation schemes remains limited despite available benefits.
findings.detail: The paper identifies that uptake of Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training is limited due to awareness barriers. Many families remain unaware of the full range of support available or how it can be adapted to their circumstances. The council is attempting to address this through improved communications and stakeholder engagement.
findings.matters: If cost management depends on increasing uptake of alternative schemes to offset rising demand, but current uptake is limited and awareness barriers persist, the strategy may not deliver expected savings.
findings.figures: No uptake figures provided
findings.quote: despite these benefits, uptake of Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training was limited due to a number of barriers, and that although existing policies provide flexibility, these options were not widely understood.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report PTBs and ITT
findings.headline: The council acknowledges significant cost pressures in school transport driven by increasing demand.
findings.detail: The scrutiny review was triggered by increasing demand for Home to School Transport. The Board recognized significant cost pressures in this area alongside increased demand for SEND support and national reforms. The council is attempting to manage rising costs by increasing uptake of Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training programs, though current uptake remains limited.
findings.matters: A council facing significant acknowledged cost pressures in a major service area where demand is increasing represents a material budget risk and sustainability concern for lenders.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided in this paper
findings.quote: the Board recognised the wider national context of increased demand for both special educational needs and disability (SEND) support and Home to School Transport, significant cost pressures, and national reforms.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation programme paused mid-planning with April 1, 2028 vesting date no longer certain
findings.detail: Government announced on 16 July 2026 a modified unitary authority proposal with 1 April 2028 vesting date. However, the Secretary of State has since announced the LGR programme has been paused for a rapid review. Transition capacity funding allocations are currently being negotiated with government, leaving timing and funding uncertain.
findings.matters: A pause mid-planning of a structural reorganisation with a 16-month vesting date creates uncertainty about transition costs, resource requirements, and execution risk—factors affecting the council's operational stability and medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: Originally scheduled vesting date: 1 April 2028; announcement of pause (date not specified in document)
findings.quote: The Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government has announced that the local government reorganisation programme has been paused while a rapid review is undertaken.

findings.headline: Oracle ERP Phase 3 payroll implementation scheduled for November 2026 with 'little contingency left' after extended testing
findings.detail: Phase 3 of Oracle (HR and Payroll for around 10,000 users) is the most complex and critical element. The second parallel payroll run was extended to meet quality thresholds, leaving minimal contingency in the programme. Live payroll migration is planned for November 2026. The paper acknowledges ongoing concerns around build quality, resourcing, and data migration, noting it is not possible to entirely mitigate against potential issues.
findings.matters: A critical payroll system implementation with extended quality cycles and depleted contingency entering its final phase creates execution risk; payroll failure is a critical service failure affecting 10,000 staff and potentially impairing the council's ability to meet statutory payments.
findings.figures: Phase 3 affects approximately 10,000 users; scheduled live payroll November 2026; contingency described as minimal
findings.quote: the second exercise was extended in order to hit the required quality threshold, leaving little contingency left in the programme.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves projected at only £3.9m by 2030, excluding additional draws required for budget balancing
findings.detail: Total strategic reserves are projected to be £3.9m by 2030, which excludes any additional draws required to balance budgets in 2026/27 or beyond. This represents the council's financial buffer after all planned mitigation, including the £70m EFS.
findings.matters: Reserves of £3.9m provide minimal buffer for a council managing complex statutory services (social care, education, safeguarding) with significant demand volatility—leaving the council vulnerable to unexpected pressures and with limited capacity to manage in-year shortfalls.
findings.figures: £3.9m strategic reserves projected by 2030 (excluding additional draws for 2026/27 and beyond)
findings.quote: Total strategic reserves are projected to be £3.9m by 2030, which excludes any additional draws required to balance budgets in 2026/27 or beyond.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review settlement 11% (below 15% national average) combined with £117.7m cumulative deficit by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 has had significant negative impact on East Sussex funding over three years. The council's Core Spending Power increase is expected to be 11%, below the national average of 15%, even with assumed Council Tax increases of 5% per annum. Despite mitigation actions, the council projects a cumulative deficit of £117.7m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A council receiving below-average funding growth while carrying a cumulative deficit approaching £118m over three years faces a structural squeeze that cannot be resolved through council tax alone—indicating either significant unplanned service reductions or continued reliance on government support.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power increase 11% vs national average 15%; cumulative deficit £117.7m by 2028/29; assumed Council Tax increases 5% per annum
findings.quote: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 has had a significant negative impact on the funding available for East Sussex over the next three years. Our Core Spending Power increase over the settlement period, as indicated by the Provisional Financial Settlement is expected to be 11%, below the national average of 15%.

findings.headline: Council requesting £70m Exceptional Financial Support to cover £55.6m 2026/27 deficit, with repeated need likely for 2027/28
findings.detail: East Sussex has submitted a request for up to £70m of capitalisation to MHCLG to balance the 2026/27 budget. The government has provided agreement in principle. However, EFS is only provided for one financial year and must be paid back. The council has notified MHCLG that without further government funding to address underlying challenges, it is likely to require EFS again for 2027/28 to deliver statutory duties.
findings.matters: A council requiring exceptional financial support to cover its operating deficit, followed by notice of likely repeat demand, signals structural imbalance between statutory obligations and available resources—a fundamental concern for any lender assessing the council's long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £55.6m deficit for 2026/27; £70m capitalisation requested; cumulative deficit of £117.7m by 2028/29
findings.quote: Our revenue budget for 2026/27 includes a £55.6m deficit, which has led us to request Exceptional Financial Support from Government... we have notified MHCLG that without further Government funding to address the challenges we face, we are likely to require EFS for 2027/28 to deliver our statutory duties.

findings.headline: Uptake of both schemes remains limited despite financial benefit and policy flexibility, due to parental concerns, awareness gaps, and practical barriers
findings.detail: The review found that families are often unaware of the flexibility available in Personal Travel Budgets (trial periods, part-week use, flexibility) and of Independent Travel Training itself. Barriers include parental anxiety about safety and independence, concerns about losing existing support if arrangements prove unsuitable, practical difficulties with work schedules and wraparound care, and in rural areas, limited public transport. The council's communications do not adequately address these barriers.
findings.matters: Low uptake of cost-saving schemes means the council is foregoing savings it could realistically achieve; addressing awareness and concerns is within council control and could materially reduce the budget overspend.
findings.figures: 214 of 5,028 pupils on Personal Travel Budget as at Q2 2025 (4.3%); only 10 of 184 families offered enhanced 65p rate have accepted
findings.quote: The Board found that awareness of both Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training remained limited among families and young people.

findings.headline: SEND home to school transport: 5,028 pupils supported as at Q2 2025; demand increased due to rising EHCP numbers
findings.detail: East Sussex has experienced significant increase in demand for SEND transport over the last three years, mirroring national trends where SEND pupils aged 0-16 account for almost three-quarters of the £2.32bn national spend. The council is responding with route optimisation, solo taxi reduction, and the Personal Travel Budget and Independent Travel Training schemes, but these can only partially offset demand growth.
findings.matters: Demand growth exceeds savings from efficiency measures, creating structural budget pressure; any new funding reform or policy change affecting EHCP or inclusion could materially worsen the position.
findings.figures: 5,028 pupils receiving Home to School Transport support as at end Q2 2025 (out of 67,097 total school pupils); national spending £2.32bn in 2023-24; national 70% increase in real terms 2015/16-2023/24
findings.quote: Mirroring the national trend, the department has seen a significant increase in demand and eligibility for Home to School Transport in the last three years (outlined in the graph below) due to an increase in the number of EHCPs being issued and the number of children eligible for Home to School Transport support.

findings.headline: Independent Travel Training shows cost avoidance of £7,700-£18,100 per pupil annually but uptake is low and a waiting list exists
findings.detail: The programme trains young people to travel independently by public transport, costing average £2,750 per pupil but displacing transport costs of £7,734-£18,112 annually. In 2024-25, 22 pupils were trained with a 96% success rate. The programme has a waiting list of 6 pupils, indicating immediate capacity to expand. Current delivery is focused on pupils aged 16+.
